source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
Their Fathers were defeated by deception and humiliation in Xibʼalbʼa; they were deceived and humiliated; tricked and cheated by the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa to end up sacrificed by Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame. Their Fathersʼ were destroyed through lies and deception which brought about their humiliation and disgrace leading to the downfall and demise which ended in their death and disappearance so that they were never heard or seen again. Yet they lived on in their Sons who lived through the remembrance and recollection of their Fathers and their noble resplendent face. Their Fathersʼ being deceived by Xibʼalbʼa to then be disgraced by Xibʼalbʼa caused them to be humiliated by Xibʼalbʼa which led to their defeat by Xibʼalbʼa that ended in their being sacrificed by those of Xibʼalbʼa who are named here as: Nim Ajawabʼ Xibʼalbʼa: Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame. It was they-the Lords of Death-who had the Fathersʼ of Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen beheaded on their Altar of Sacrifice that stood beside their Sacrificial Ballcourt of Ballcourt Sacrifice in Xibʼalbʼa that is known to one and all as the place known as: Pusbʼal Chaaj.

Everything the Sons of Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu did came out well since they were born with the knowledge to do all they came to do for they were just Nawinaq as it is said of those Winaq who were born to be Nawales and so it was that they were the kʼexel of their Fathersʼ; Fathersʼ whose Sons were their replacements; Fathers who descended down into Xibʼalbʼa to follow the Black Road that led to their Death; for their Fathers were sacrificed and buried beside the ballcourt in Xibʼalbʼa by the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa: Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame.

And so it was that Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen were great knowers-nimaʼq etaʼmanel-great seers; knowing everything clearly, seeing everything clearly. And what they knew clearly and what they saw clearly was everything there was to be seen and known as the replacements-kʼexel of Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu-their Fathers so that they-Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen-came to know all and see all as great knowers and great seers: nimaʼq etaʼmanel.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
And this they held within them as their way of knowing and seeing; they knew and saw this from the very beginning; from the time they were borne into the world for they were their Fathersʼ replacements; they were their Fathersʼ successors; they were their Fathersʼ descendants; their Fathersʼ heirs: kʼexel.

Yet when their Younger Brothers were born the all knowing ways of Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen disappeared. When their Younger Brothers; Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej were born then the all seeing ways of Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen came to an end; their knowledge, their wisdom no longer came forth as it had always come forth in the past.

This was just because of their envy; this was just because of their red-faced anger that they lost what was given to them at birth as a gift.

Yet it was only upon them-the Older Brothers-that fell their resentment and anger; it was their own ill-will and resentment that fell back on them; it was just their very own envy and jealousy that turned their hearts towards ill-will and hatred that they turned towards their Younger Brothers and this is what would cause their downfall and defeat; the defeat and downfall of Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen. For it would be the death and destruction of their Older Brothers that would be brought about by their great reversal of destiny caused and created by their Younger Brothers, Junajpu, IxBʼalamkej. And this is the story that will be told here.

Older Brothers; Younger Brothers Birds Blown-down in the Forest Birds Eaten-up in the Kitchen Food not Shared; Life not Lived

There Younger Brothers brought home the birds they hunted with their blowguns to give them to their Grandmother who cooked them up to feed them to their Older Brothers.

This is what the Younger Brothers did; they just brought home the birds they hunted up on the Mountain; they brought home birds every day; day after day they brought home birds so that their Grandmother could feed her Boys; her Grandsons; the Boys who were the Sons of Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu.

Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej brought home the food that was needed to feed those who had to be fed just like their Mother IxKikʼ had been asked to do a long time ago.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
But the Older Brothers showed them no thanks they just treated their Younger Brothers like servants, as if they were their ʼboysʼ. That is how they treated Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej never practiced ʼwitchcraftʼ on them, never did they try to take their Older Brothers down; for certainly they could have; they could have done them harm; but they didnʼt do them any harm through twisting-up ʼgrass dollsʼ to bring about their downfall; to bring about the destruction of their adversary; to cause the death and demise of their enemy.

Mawi bʼanoj xepoysaxik kumal ri Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

They didnʼt get mad; they didnʼt get angry because they knew that was no way to live life. It was just getting up at dawn to shoulder their blowguns that the two Younger Brothers did; it was just wandering about on the mountain-pa juyubʼ taking down birds out of the trees that the Two Boys, Two Sons did; this is how they spent their every day-juta qʼij.

This was what they did because this is what they were born to do; they were those who were born to serve others is what they were born to do. They brought home the food to feed their Older Brothers; their Grandmother; and their Mother.

Feeding those who had to be fed is what fell on the Younger Brothers, Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej who shouldered their blowguns at dawn to walk out of the house and then up into the mountains as they did every day.

A New Way of Life; A New Way of Living Seeking a Way Out of Abuse and Oppression

Nourishing and nurturing others was just their burden to bear; the burden that was theirs was their burden to bear; the burden they took up to bear every day; the sacred burden they took it up on their shoulders and carried across the Sky; the sacred burden of service the bore across the Face of the Earth like the Sun that Day-Keepers bear as Cargadores del Sol; Cargadores del Tiempo. This is the Sacred Burden of each and everyoneʼs calling that the Boys bear-up as the Providers and Sustainers of their Family. After all the Older Brothers work hard; they suffer at what they do and the Ancient Word make certain that we know this.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
The Mother-Fathers of the Ancient Word want to make sure that these Noble Lords are ʼhardʼ which is to say they ʼwork hardʼ but they donʼt share their sustenance which in the Maya World is the ʼworst transgressionʼ one could possibly commit against others. So be it!

They knew what was theirs in life and had always been content to be those who brought home the birds that their Grandmother stewed up for their Older Brothers who made their Grandmother content with all that they did to warm her heart. Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej did what they did because they knew what they needed to do to rearrange their way of life and the household into which theyʼd been born and has always lived.

The time had come to change their life by following their nawal genius for living life; a magical way of living life that came so naturally to them. A way of living life they were born into to provide and sustain others with all they needed to live by being fed with that which they had always been fed. But was this the life they were meant to live or was it the life lived to fulfill the needs of others? These Younger Brothers knew the time had come to change their life; and, they knew it was time to transform the way their life was lived in the House of their Father; the Home of their Grandmother.

The time had come to find out what was truly theirs in life in order to live out their life in ways that would to fulfill their destiny on the Face of the Earth there beneath the Sky. But what this destiny of theirs way they really did not know; not yet. So, so they used their cunning and clever imagination to come up with a way to find out what truly was theirs in life. To do this they would do what all tricksters do and that was to create some sort of disruption; to concoct some sort of disturbance that enabled the Boys; the Sons; the Twins to move about in new ways and in new directions so they could bring their lives to fruition.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
This is the story of what they came to say and do in order to change and transform the way life was lived for all those who came to live walking in their footsteps across the Face of the Earth. So letʼs get moving in the direction of those footsteps of the Hero Twins and the powerful places they take those who are willing to sacrifice themselves to living the ʼhardʼ life for the greater good of the Pueblo; for liberation of its many, many People. Because, as we will come to see, these Boys of a single Mother; these Sons of murdered Fathers; the Twins of a Family destroyed by grief and loss caused by death and destruction were those who will liberate their Pueblo from the tyranny of the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa.

The Hero Twins will destroy the Lords of Death and their violent intimidating rule over the People who live on the Face of the Earth. These Boys are true liberators of the oppressed and this is why the Popol Wuj-despite being the National Book of Guatemala-is never read in Guatemala not taught in any Public Forums. Popol Wuj is a very dangerous book for those who depend on ʼBoys going to the Mountain to bring back the wealth of the Wildernessʼ in order to feed those who live in the ease of ancestral privilege whoʼs only responsibility it to ʼwarm the heart of Grandmotherʼ in order to cheer her soul and its loss.

This is the paradox of Mythos because there is nothing wrong with ʼwarming the heart of Grandmotherʼ to console her life of constant death and loss of her loved ones. This is of the highest moral order yet if this means sacrificing the joy and happiness of the other People of the Pueblo then we have a problem. Popol Wuj asks us to contemplate what is most important to the Pueblo so that they might prosper in the Arts as the Monkey Twins do. Myths are always radical critiques of the hierarchical rule of a Nation of People; Myths always question the needs of the Lords and Rulers in the context of those Women and Men; Girls and Boys; Trees and Animals; Mountains and Streams; Lakes and Seas; Earth and Sky over which they rule.

body:
This is why Popol Wuj is so vital revolutionary literature to our re-imagination of life, death, and rebirth in las Américas because it takes us back to before the ʼarrival of strangersʼ on the Caribbean Coast known as the Coming Out Place of the Sun. Popol Wuj takes us back to this Sacred Place of Emergence on the Yucatan Peninsula where the Kʼicheʼ Maya traveled in Sacred Journeys to watch and wait for the Sun to Dawn at the Coming Out Place of the Sun. This is where the Castilians will emerge out of the East floating across the Sea on clouds of ʼas ifʼ they were the return of those Divine Twins Heart of the Sky; Heart of the Earth; Heart of Lake; Heart of the Sea. There is no hope of understanding European History if we donʼt enter the Ancient Word of Mesoamerican Myth. We must enter the Mesoamerica World through their Mythos known as Popol Wuj. For it is in this Ancestral Account we experience Mesoamerican critical theory of Noble Rule and its use of Sacrifice to terrify the Pueblo by intimidating the People. This is coming. This is coming to be told right here in this Book of Pueblo known to the Kʼicheʼ Maya Scribes who wrote it as Popol Wuj; the Council Book; the Book of Counsel. So letʼs get moving to prove to ourselves we cannot understand the Maya People as a Mesoamerican Pueblo unless we develop a deep understanding of the Ancient Word of Popol Wuj. Jo, Jo; Jo Junam Jo…Letʼs go, letʼs go; letʼs get going together… They just went ʼblow-gunningʼ up on the mountainside which is what they did each and every day. Xa kʼu wubʼanik chi kibʼano juta qʼij.

They were not well loved by their Grandmother, Ixmuqane nor by Jun Bʼatzʼ nor Jun Chowen. They were never given any of the food that they brought home with them; the birds they shared with their Elder Brothers were not shared with them.

It was only after Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen had eaten that the Younger Brothers were allowed to enter beside their Grandmotherʼs fire that burned in her three-stone-hearth; but then there was nothing left for them to eat.

body:
The Boys, the Sons, the Twins didnʼt get all burnt up; they didnʼt get all red- faced mad; no they didnʼt become angry of sad, no. No, they didnʼt do that at all; instead they just looked at it as they were taught to do and then took it like they had always done; and, would continue to do.

They understood the nature of their situation; they understood the nature of their condition: kikʼojeʼik.

They saw their existence just as it was; they knew what was required from them and their mother who brought her engendered sons into life as the woman; as the wife of Jun Junajpu.

This was just the way it was in a world with oppressive ways of submitting others to oppression and abuse to live out a submissive experience of existence on the Face of the Earth. They brought back the birds they hunted everyday when they came down from the mountain. All of which were finished off by Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen who ate all that they were given while always being hungry for more. And so it was that there was never anything left for the two of them, Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej to chew- up. But that is the way it was in this ancient ancestral account that there was no way of changing or transforming to find a way out. Just playing their flutes, just singing their songs was what they did all day long; just the two of them, Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen, warming the heart of their Grandmother; as their Fathers asked them to do.

Just warming their Grandmotherʼs heart was what was theirs to do in life. And perhaps it was because of this that they resented having their Younger Brothers around to do what they did best which was to play music and make merry to make their Grandmother smile and laugh.

So what else could they do as Younger Brothers of Older Brother like this other than bide their time knowing that someday their chance would come to show their Grandmother that they too could bring contentment and happiness to her life and not just the birds they took down from tree tops with their magic blowguns that brought their Older Brothersʼ sustenance out of the tree tops with their blowgun magic that left the birds flat on their backs on the ground down below.

body:
What else could they do than enjoy their Older Brothers music and all that they did to make their Grandmotherʼs heart as warm as a warm-hearted Grandmother could be?

Just flute; just song is all that they did; those named Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen. This was when Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej came down off the mountain like they always did, only this time they didnʼt bring anything home with them.

This then was when they came in without a single bird; when they came in with nothing; nothing at all.

Not one bird did they bring in with them when they came down from the mountain; not one bird was hanging off the belt of those Boysʼ when they came in to house of their Grandmother; when they came home with nothing; nothing at all; when they didnʼt bring a thing home when they came home with nothing at all; nothing to roast; nothing to cook; nothing to eat; just nothing, nothing at all.

This just burned up the Old Woman; furious is what she was as she erupted red-faced with anger that only she knew: “Why havenʼt you brought back any birds?” she demanded of Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej. This then was when they ʼmade their wordsʼ for her, as agreed upon by the two of them after talking council with one another.

And so they said: “Well it is like this, you esteemed Grandmother of ours-Ix Qatiʼt our birds just got hung-up-xa mixetanatobʼ in the treetop; our birds just got snagged in the branches. There is just no way that we can climb-up there to bring them down; oh you, our Grandmother; Ix Qatiʼt.” “So, we wish to ask our ʼOlder Brothers-Qatzʼ that they might go with us, to perhaps climb-up in the tree to bring the birds down; the birds caught in the branches; the birds snagged up in the limbs,” they said then to their Grandmother there in the patio of her house.

They said what they said to their Grandmother where their Older Brothers could hear what they said.

body:
And, they did, their Older Brothers did hear what was said for them to hear of the words the Boys prepared so well for their Grandmother to hear there where they could be heard by their Older Brothers because they answered right away. “Utz bʼa la, very well, we will go with you at dawn!” Answered their Older Brothers-Katz without speaking to their Grandmother before speaking to their Younger Brothers-Kichaqʼ who were happy as could be that their Older Brothers were going to accompany them up on the mountain at dawn.

And that was that for them, the Artisan Twins; the Monkey Twins; those Artists; those Artisans who may well have tasted their own downfall that was their defeat that was their demise like others who had hungered; others who had hankered for just a taste of a brazed piece of meat to eat as a tasty, tasty treat… This then was when they, Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej, brought forth their imaginative thinking as companions who acted as one by gathering together their thoughts; thoughts that would bring about the defeat of their Older Brothers; Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen.

This was when Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej spoke between one another about their defeat of Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen. “We will just transform their nature, their condition; their way of being- kikʼojeʼik! This is our word, our truth; for this is all we have to say; may it reveal the longing within us; may it speak of our appetite; may it tell the truth of our hunger-E upam qatzij.”

“So be it! Ta chuxoq! May it come to be because of the great suffering they have caused us! They wanted us to die; they just wanted that we should disappear, us, their Younger Brothers.”

“They treated us just like vassals; we were seen as servants in their eyes, servants who did as they ordered; we were expected to provide for their every need so that ʼpoco a pocoʼ we came to be seen by them as their boys-kʼeje ri ala-we, their servants; and, they, our masters!” “This is how they treated us so that in their eyes we were seen as dutiful subjects; born to be obedient; born to be punished; born to serve them here in their Fathersʼ house; here in their Grandmothersʼ home.”

body:
And so it shall be that in this same way we shall defeat them; we shall make a fine example of them!” This then is what they said when they took council with one-an-other there as true companions, as complements of one-the-other as it is said; as complementary twins; as cooperative brothers; as collaborative twin brothers-kibʼil kibʼ kikabʼichal.

Under the Yellow Tree;

Chuxeʼ Qʼan Cheʼ;

Beneath the Big Yellow Tree

This then was when they went walking over there to where the Yellow Tree stood; over where they would come to the Yellow Tree; Qʼan Teʼ ubʼiʼ; Qʼanteʼ ubʼi: Yellow Tree is its name Qʼan Teʼ as it was once known.

Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej; the Younger Brothers-Kichaqʼ went walking towards the Yellow Tree accompanied by their Older Brothers-Katz.

They walked along testing their skills as they made their way walking just trying their luck with the blowguns on the innumerable birds there in the forest kechʼititik-chittering away in the treetops especially there beneath the Yellow Tree where they now stood looking up at all the birds they heard chirping and chattering in its limbs.

Yet despite the countless birds they came upon there in the Big Yellow Tree not ʼone of themʼ fell from where they were caught snared in the branches; not ʼone of themʼ flopped down from the top where they were snagged in the limbs of the Yellow Tree below which the Older Brothers had arrived after accompanying their Younger Brothers as they made their way afoot in the forest with its many trees.

Infinite quantities of birds were there in the forest just chittering; just chattering up in the treetops but none more than the Qʼan Teʼ ; the Yellow Tree; the Dye Tree known as Qʼan Teʼ.

body:
Their Older Brothers were awestruck by the great multitude of birds they saw there. But of all the great many birds they saw, and of all the great many birds that now lay motionless in the limbs high up in this Great Tree not one of them fell from where they lay stunned in the branches of the Yellow Tree; the Yellow Tree below which the Younger Brothers now stood with their Older Brothers. “Our birds just wonʼt fall! Why donʼt the two of you just climb up into its branches to bring them down from where they are snared in the limbs,” they said to their Older Brothers-Katz.

“Utz bʼa la, very well then,” said the Older Brothers-ri Katz-to the Younger Brothers-ki Chaqʼ. As soon as Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen climbed up into the tree it instantly began growing; and, as soon as it began growing so too did it begin to swell; and, as soon as it began to swell so too did its great girth begin to bulge-sipoj upam.

It was then that the two Older Brothers wished to come down; but they couldnʼt come right back down, because the two of them, Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen, were now high up in the branches of this now Giant Yellow Tree-Qʼan Teʼ.

That was when they called down from where they were doing their best to hang on to the giant branches of this now enormous tree.

“How can we hold on, You, Our Little Brothers-Ix Qachaq? How can we hold on to this tree? Please, Little Brothers; help us Boys-toqʼobʼ qawach-pity us Little Brothers! Please, forgive us Boys-toqʼobʼ qawach-por fa, do something to save us because this tree is so very, very terrifying, as you can see, you, our Little Brother-Ix Qachaqʼ it is such a Big, Big Tree that is just getting bigger and bigger all the time!” They called out as they screamed down from high in the branches of that Big Yellow Tree.

This then was when Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej yelled up to them: “Donʼt worry; Itʼs alright, just untie the long sash of your pants-chikiraʼ iwex, chixima xe ipam- just tie the sash of your pants around your waist and then let the ends of your sash hang down long; just let them hand down your backside, like a tail, then you will be able to move about with ease in the branches of the tree.”

body:
This was what they were told to do by their Younger Brothers-Kichaqʼ when the Older Brothers-Katz called down from high up in the branches of the Qʼan Teʼ. “We! Fine!” called down the Older Brothers from high up in the tree. They answered back as they pulled on the free ends of their long sashes and then wrapped the sash around their waist so that instead of having two ends of the sash hanging down the front they wrapped and bound their sash so that it was left with only one long end that they tied off ʼjust soʼ that it hung down their backside nice and long. Once they finished their work wrapping and binding each of their sashes was knotted so that it hung down the back long and loose. Then Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej blew; the two blew…puuj…puuj…and all of a sudden, just like that, those long flowing sashes of theirs transformed into two long flowing tails-kije; and then in an instant-xa pu jusu; and then in a flash; in just a flicker…puuj…puuj…in just a flash their sash became a long tail; in a flash their sash became the tail that now hung down their back like the monkey tail it had suddenly become; those Two Young Men who had been their Older Brothers had been transformed in an instant into Spider Monkeys-Kʼoy. This then was when they went through the trees of Small Mountains; Big Mountains making their way through the forest now howling out as they swung through the limbs of the trees with the greatest of ease. This is how Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen were defeated by Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej. It was just their magical powers of transformation that made it so; it was just their nawal powers that caused Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen to be magically transformed into Spider Monkeys: Kʼoy.

Spider Monkeys: Kʼoy It was these Spider Monkeys who now playfully hung in the Qʼan Teʼ by their long arms and long legs with four hands and long, long tail that they used most gracefully to hang from the limbs and branches of this enormous tree that they now moved through with the greatest of ease. Their being saved was no longer in question. They werenʼt worried a bit anymore because they could grab hold and hang on with four hands now and all as if they had somehow done this before!

body:
Now, with their nature transformed and their condition changed the appearance of the two Older Brothers had become that of another more mischievous essence; which was that of the Spider Monkey or Kʼoy as these badly-behaved tricksters are known to this day; bothersome greedy creatures, real nuisance in the jungle forest especially for those who grew milpas of cacao and maize or groves of fruit trees.

But what could be done now? It was too late to go back to who and how and what they once were just a short time ago; the Elder Brothers were now Kʼoy just as their Younger Brothers had conceived and imagined with their Naʼoj: their Nawal Knowing.

And so it was that those Two Spider Monkeys went swinging off through the trees as the animals they had become. For it was they who now looked just exactly like they had always acted with their Younger Brothers which was just exactly how these irritated looking furry-faced fuzzy-headed Boys appeared to be; monkeys of the forest, creatures of the trees-xa kʼoy xkiwachibʼey chik! They took on the look as they matched the exact appearance of Spider Monkeys who went swinging through the canopy; just flying through the trees of the Small Mountains, Big Mountains.

They moved with ease through the branches of the trees howling out as they hurled themselves about the forest up through the limbs of the treetops swinging with both hands and feet as they moved through the forest like the breeze in the trees.

And so it was Jun Bʼatzʼ Jun Chowen looked like the Spider Monkeys they became; like the Spider Monkeys they now were; like the Spider Monkeys they were meant to be; those wild animals who made their home in the trees. Just like that Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen were defeated by JunAjPu, IxBʼalamKiej.

body:
It was just their magical powers of transformation-kinawal that made it so; it was their superior genius and inspired imagination that gave them their ancestral powers of transformation which bestowed upon them the ability to change themselves into anything they need to be to ʼget the job doʼ and so it was they could transform other into whatever it was those being truly were in their heart, in their soul so that they transformed into who or what they truly were; and it was all done in an instant; for truly they were Nawal Winaq known also as Nawinaq.

Whatever could have Happened to Our Older Brothers; they looked just like Animals When they climbed up into the Trees

So then they returned home. They were determined to speak to their Grandmother as soon as they returned home. And so they walked straight over to the Old Woman who was waiting there to speak with them as soon as they arrived back home; and so it was that they spoke with their Grandmother and their Mother.

When they arrived then at their home, they immediately went to speak then with their Grandmother and their Mother. This is what they did when they returned home to their Grandmotherʼs Sitio where they lived together in their Family Compound with its fruit trees and herb patch; potted plants and fruit trees; wash basin and firewood. The Boys; the Sons; the Twins well, what else could they do but go over to their Grandmother and Mother. They went to talk to them about their Older Brothers and how they had ʼjustʼ changed face and how that ʼfaceʼ was now a Spider Monkey face-xa Kʼoy xkiwachibʼej chik-they said.

Junajpu Kʼoy Ancient Animal Ancestors Monkey Boy; Monkey Man

They just sang and played this ancient, ancestral song of the ancient, animal ancestors calling them forth so that they might come dancing in so Grandmother could prove she was able to hold back her laughter and win the victory that was certainly hers to be won so that her Grandsons could return home to warm her heart like they had done for so long by playing their music and singing their songs.

body:
It was just a test to see if she could keep from laughing at these entertaining Young Men, her Grandsons, who had made her laugh so very easily her whole life long with the funny ways they acted and the silly things they said that always warmed their Grandmotherʼs heart while lifting her spirits and the heavy weight of loss she felt deep down in her soul for the grief she knew so well amongst a family where Lords of Death claimed both the young and the old.

But there was no greater loss felt by this Mother of Noble Sons than the grief she faced day to day because of the death and disappearance; defeat and demise of her beloved Ball- Playing Sons whoʼs sacrifice by Xibʼalbʼa came as a catastrophic sort of shock experienced as a soul shattering surprise. Grandmother survived it all through her Grandsons who picked up the pieces and put their life back together by monkey-ing around make fun where there was none.

If anyone could make Grandmother laugh it most definitely these Twin Grandsons of the Old Women. But it was time to get over all of that and do what was asked of her as the Great Matriarch of the Maize People who had to show everyone that life wasnʼt always a bunch of laughs nor was death something to be held on to in a World where life goes on and the next generation might just be the best that there ever was; better than ever before so there is no time waste crying over what canʼt be changed and might just be the very thing that opens the door opportunities never ever imagined before. It was time for the Old Woman to show what it meant to be ʼhardʼ like a kernel of maize; ʼhardʼ like cacao. This was it; game on; it was time to throw down the rubberball into play.

body:
“You, our Grandmother, whatever could have happened to our Older Brothers-Qatz-for they ʼinstantly took on a new lookʼ as it is said ʼthey took on a new image; a new face; a new way of beingʼ when they took off into the mountains looking just like animals-chikop; they looked just like animals when we last saw them climbing up through the trees,” they said. “If you did something to your Older Brothers; if you caused them to be lost to me so that I might no longer see them; if you somehow caused me ruin or for some reason caused me disgrace! I hope you havenʼt done something like that to your Older Brothers, you my precious Grandsons of mine; you, my beloved Descendants of mine-Ix Wi. I hope it is not something like that you have done to me, your Grandmother,” said the Grandmother-ri Atiʼt-the Old Woman to Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej. “Donʼt be sad, you Our Grandmother-Mixbʼisonik, Ix Qatiʼt, donʼt be worried, you Our Grandmother, for you will see their faces again, the faces of our Older Brothers, you will see them again because they will return here; they will return again.” “They will most certainly return and when they return their return will ʼjustʼ be a test for you, ʼjustʼ a trial for you, an ordeal for you; you, our Grandmother; Ix Qatiʼt.” “It is a simple matter; it is just a simple matter of you not laughing at them when they come in; when they come in dancing.”

“This is just a trial; just a test of sorts, a kind of travail; for its is just a test; just a question of their destiny; a question of their future that is a question of their fate; so whatever you do, donʼt laugh when they come back in; because when they come back in they will come in dancing,” they said then when they spoke to their Grandmother there in the ʼpatio or sitioʼ of her home; the ʼsitio or patioʼ of her Sons who died in Xibʼalbʼa.

When they took up their flute and drum Grandmother sat down beside them in the patio there in front of her family home anticipating the arrival of those who were sure to return to where they came from as Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej played away on their flute in order to call in their Older Brothers back with their tune; coaxing them back home with their song.

body:
And so it was Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej who began to play a song; they began to play a song on their flute; the song they played right away was the melody known a Junajpu Kʼoy, the Original Ancestral Spider Monkey Song as it is known, Junajpu Kʼoy; they played it on their flutes first; then they sung as song; then they drummed it out as the beat of this ancient ancestral ʼsonʼ.

Then the two of them, Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej, just sang it as they sung it out in song; they just played it on their flute; they piped it for the ancient, ancient tune that it was; they just drummed it out when they drummed it on their drum; xebʼixanik; xesuʼanik; xeqʼojomanik; they sung it, they sang it; they piped it, they played it; they drummed it, they just hummed it so that it rang out in the mountains and hills calling their Monkey Twin Brothers back home. This was when they took up their flute and drum to play their enchanting tune in order to sing their enticing song along with the Old Woman who came in to sit with them there in the patio; and so they played on their flute-xul, they just piped on their cane flute-aaj su, aaj-xu; they just drummed on their double-headed drum-qʼojom as they sang; as they sung out their sweet sonorous song-bʼix; their summons of the Sons who came swinging back home charmed by the beguiling melody of Junajpu Kʼoy.

And so it was that they just played their tune to call them in, the Boys who were know Kʼoy who came swinging in from afar as they felt the call of this ancient, ancestral incantation that was played just for them to come in from the wild; the musicians just called them in with their mesmerizing melody; calling them back home with their enchanting flute upon which they played their captivating song: Junajpu Kʼoy.

Junajpu Kʼoy was the Ancient Ancestral Spider Monkey Song that was the name of the tune they played up into the forest crying out, calling out for the Older Brothers to return; to come home to the one and only place they had ever known.

body:
Junajpu Kʼoy Song of Enchantment; Ancient Ancestral Son They sang them down from the trees; they called them out of the forest with their ancestorsʼ ancient ancestral tune; they beckoned them in from the mountainside with the mesmerizing melody known to all as Junajpu Kʼoy; an enchanting song if ever there was an incantation with the strength to call the Boys back home and into their house, out of the forest, down from the trees and into their Grandmotherʼs home.

This spellbinding song was now played and sung to call them in dancing to this ancestral incantation of the Ancient Ancestral Spider Monkey Song: Junajpu Kʼoy was its name; the name of the invocation played as enchantment to invoke the Ancestral Soul of the Ancient Ones.

Junajpu Kʼoy was the name of the tune that they piped away on their flute; it was the rhythm they drummed away at on their drum; it was the song they sang away at their Ancient Ancestral Spider Monkey Song: Junajpu Kʼoy is its name. Their effort of ancestral enchantment began to work for their incantation was heard near and far.

Before long the Monkey Twins came in dancing as they danced into the patio of Grandmotherʼs family compound. It was then when the two of them returned; when the two of them arrived there where the Boys played and Grandmother watched the Monkey Boys as they danced now completely captivated by their song; it was then that the Kʼoy-Spider Monkeys entered their song and dance known as Junajpu Kʼoy with its tempting tempo; its beguiling beat;

its mesmerizing melody that got the dancers dancing with its enchanting allure; its soul summons of sumptuous sound.

This then was when Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen came in dancing as they came dancing along to the piping; to the singing of their song that grabbed hold of them and would not let then go; a melody, a song, a tune that wouldnʼt leave them alone.

body:
They just danced round and round spellbound by this song that was played just for them; a song sung just for them; an ancestral song played and sung for a long, long time as a song that was a ʼsonʼ that was played just for them; Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen who now danced about with pure joy to the song that was theirs and theirs alone to sing and dance: Junajpu Kʼoy.

And so then their Grandmother saw them; and when the Old Woman saw their faces that looked so dirty and scruffy; so unclean, so unkempt she could help but smile a bit; they looked so very funny; really, the way they swirled and spun about thumping their bottom and rubbing their tummy.

The faces they made and the way they danced was more than enough to make Grandma break into big bright smile and when she smiled she couldnʼt help but chuckle, just a bit; not too much. But then as she watched she couldnʼt help herself she just had to laugh and once she laughed a little she just let herself laugh a lot so this was when she started laughing; there was no stopping her laughter. Here and now; before and after the Old Woman just enjoyed her laughter while watching the Monkey Boys dancing all about with one another. And so it was that the Old Woman laughed and laughed the kind of laughter that came so easy to her; for this was the Grandmother whoʼs Boys lived to make their Grandmother laugh.

The Old Woman laughed as she always laughed because that is what she did when her Boys danced their dances and sang their songs and played around in the patio to warm her heart.

Grandmother simply ʼcouldʼ not control that which she thought she ʼshouldʼ not control because of the funny things those dancers did to tempt her laughter; laughter that came so natural to her; as natural as it was for her Grandsonsʼ piping hot tunes on their flutes, drumming blazing rhythms on their drums, and singing soulful songs with their cheerful voices all of which were performed to warm their Grandmotherʼs heart.

body:
No doubt this was going to be much more of an ordeal than the Old Woman could have imagined or thought possible. Surely she could control her laughter. Maybe not now but certainly the next time when this test turned to another chapter.

Immediately they-the Monkey Boys-Kʼoy-took off, in an instant they were gone; climbing up through the branches of the trees they flew right back up into the forest to then shoot straight up into the canopy.

Once they were out and away in the wilderness-pa juyubʼ no longer could their faces be seen by anyone who could be made to laugh uncontrollably but that didnʼt stop them from goofing around anyway because that was their nature; that is the way they were by nature; that was the very essence of who and how they were formed and shaped to be in the funny world in which the lived in and upon the Sky-Earth.

Up and away they went swinging as they swung along until they returned to the Forest-Kʼechelaj from where they had come before they had been summoned by the enthralling enchantment of their song; the beguiling beckoning of their beat; the strident summons of their soul; the alluring allure of their ancient, ancestral song, Junajpu Kʼoy.

Control your Laughter: Show Humility; Show Grace Control your Laughter: Show Nobility; Show Place Control your Laughter: Embody Serenity; Ensoul Sacred Space

In no time they were back to where they had come before they had been humiliated by the laughter of their Grandmother; before they had been called into the patio of the house that had been their home where they were laughed at hysterically by their Grandmother. Those Monkey Boys had come and gone quicker and faster than any of them could have or would have ever thought or imagined possible for Monkey Boys who are quick and fast by the very nature of their condition.

body:
Surely their beloved Grandmother ʼcouldʼ do better than that; or, perhaps ʼshouldʼ do better than that if only she ʼwouldʼ do better than that. If onlyʼ she ʼcouldʼ make up her mind to really do better than her beloved Boys now wished she ʼwouldʼ as they thought she ʼshouldʼ at least for them like they now hoped she ʼwouldʼ; if only she ʼcouldʼ do better than she ʼshouldʼ have done already.

But their Grandmother was an Old Women who ʼwouldʼ always fall easily into laughter unless she ʼcouldʼ stay calm and focused in order to keep her ʼeye on the prizeʼ and her mind on what was at stake right here in her House as all Old Woman probably ʼshouldʼ in a situation like this.

But who ʼcouldʼ ever say what a Grandmother ʼwouldʼ do when completely ʼtakenʼ by a Dance Performance like that hilarious performance her Monkey Boys had just presented to her just a moment ago. What ʼcouldʼ one do? What ʼshouldʼ one do? Most importantly what ʼwouldʼ the Monkey Boys do if their Grandmother ʼcouldnʼtʼ control her laughter; of simply ʼwouldnʼtʼ control her laughter as they most certainly thought she ʼshouldʼ do… Oh, dear reader, what on Earth does this mean? This laughter that we experienced with the Lords of Death when they almost ʼdieʼ from laughter when Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu do what they do in the ʼEntrance Wayʼ of Xibʼalbʼa and then on the ʼHot Benchʼ that burns their ʼbuttʼ bad. This laughing at others is very much a big part of Maya life. Making others laugh is a vital aspect of Maya Laugh but it must be done with humility and grace never crass or vulgar; never too truthful that it causes disgrace. This is what is going on here in mythic metaphorical ways that reveal the ʼserious playʼ of the Popol Wuj in a seriously sort of funny way.

Junajpu Kʼoy In Come Dancing the Monkey Boys Ancient Ancestral Mountain Twins Ancient Ancestral Grandsons

body:
“What have you done, you our beloved Grandmother? Just four times will we test you; just three more times will we call them in out of the forest with our flute, with our song; so just do what you must do to ʼpardonʼ your laughter. We are going to try again!” said Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej. So then they called them in with their flute; it wasnʼt long for their song to call them in dancing; when they return they return dancing along.

They danced right on into the patio, onto the terraza they came dancing; just dancing all around they came in prancing all about when they came in dancing to the song; that was the ʼsonʼ; that was the dance known as Junajpu Kʼoy.

Their song that was their dance; with its tempo; with its timing; with its rhythm; with its rhyming; its calling; its crying; its racing; its chasing; its miming; its climbing; this wild, wild dance of the hunt thus the name Jun Aj Pu Kʼoy-Ancient Ancestral One Monkey Man-One Hunter Spider Monkey: Jun AjPubʼ Kʼoy.

This is the Dance that is the Song that the Boys sing as the song that is sung to call Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen in to dance their dance of the hunt; their dance that is danced as a hunt that is a chase. This is what happens in ʼcourtyardʼ of Grandmotherʼs House where ʼOne Hunter-Jun Ajpuʼ chases the Spider Monkeys-Kʼoy all about.

They just danced their Spider Monkey dance by dancing their ancestral dance Junajpu Kʼoy with elegance and grace; this dance that was a chase that they danced as they ran; as they race; as they danced by dancing all-around their Grandmotherʼs place.

They came in dancing right there as they danced onto the terraza that was at the center of the house; there in el sitio; there in the compound where the Monkeys came in dancing when they danced all around. When they danced entranced by the sound of the song; captivated by the flute; charmed by the drum they just pranced about dancing as they danced about prancing; enchanted by their song: Junajpu Kʼoy.

body:
There in the patio of Grandmotherʼs house is where Grandmother now sat where the Monkey Boys now danced up and down while climbing all around as they raced about and chased about as they ran after one another up and down the walls that surrounded the house then back out on the patio of Grandmotherʼs great house.

Those named Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej are also known One Hunter and Little Jaguar-Deer; spoken of as One Hunter; One Blowgun Boy; those who are the Hunter and the Hunted; Jaguar- Deer; those of Forest beside the Milpa where this dance takes place.

It was these who were those who played out this Ancient Ancestral Hunting Song of Jun- Ajpu, Ix-Bʼalam-Kej and it was they who sang and played; piped and drummed out the rhythm of the song that called down the Spider Monkey Boys to dance all around; all around the patio, up along the crown; on the crest high up on the walls, there was nowhere these dancers didnʼt go for it was just in their nature to go where the chase carried them about. They just swung from the beams on terrace walls from where they climbed up on top of Grandmotherʼs House to then start over again. They just danced dancing up and down as they pranced in and out of the patio where they whirled all-around and twirled all about to the ancient ancestral tune known as Junajpu Kʼoy the song that was the son that echoed all around as it bounced up and down to resound all about the Old Womanʼs familial compound.

Entranced by the spellbinding sound they just danced and danced, when they came in dancing all about as they danced round and round while climbing up and down the posts and pillars of Grandmotherʼs House. Those Monkey Twins really knew how to dance their dance that their Younger Brothers now played in the most delightful way to enchant, to enthrall; to beguile, to bewitch those who were summoned by song sung to be danced as Jun AjPu Kʼoy. The Old Woman was thrilled by all they did as they danced about the center of her house.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
It didnʼt take much to tempt the laughter of their Grandmother who had a hard time containing her laughter because of the funny ways her Boys acted and all the goofy things they did to amuse the Old Woman to whom laughing and laughter came so natural.

Before she knew what was happening the Old Woman was doubled over laughing; laughing with uncontrollable laughter causing tears to well-up in the corner of her eyes from the laughter that came so easily to those who were born and raised on lament and laughter; weeping and sobbing one minute that were jokesterʼs loving laughter; tricksters mocking mirth.

This was just their natural condition, the way they were made to be; the two of them, the Monkey Twins; her Grandsons-Iwiey Mam her constant companions since they were wee little newborn infants who made their Grandmother smile and laugh with their silly ways they acted and the silly faces they made; the funny sort of hilarious things they did.

Truly hilarious were the funny faces they made that came from the fuzzy faces of these Monkey Boys and the laughable way that, that ʼlittle thingʼ that hung down below their bellies swung about; and, their incessant moving tails that constantly waved up around their heads and all around their chest to just swirl up and around their wild-eyed, big-eared fuzzy-heads. They were a sight to see that would make anyone laugh; so funny were their silly ways that poor Grandma had no chance. So that then was when they came in dancing again the funny, funny way they did that instantly made the Old Woman laugh even more than before not knowing she had lost the wager. What could she do about these Boys of hers and their hilarious behavior that warmed her heart so?

So now when she laughed she just kept on laughing and laughing; there was no stopping her laughter; the uproarious laughter of Grandmother; the Old Woman.

body:
And so it was and so it seemed to be that no matter what those Boys did it tempted Grandmotherʼs laughter; so that she laughed the kind of laughter that just kept her laughing. This was something storytellers would repeat over and over by telling the story of Junajpu Kʼoy again and again; a story about the easy going way of the Old Womanʼs laughing her uncontrollable laughter.

For it was Grandmotherʼs easy going laughter that drove the Monkey Twins back up into the many trees of the forest; when they swung back up onto the mountainside where they live to this day just on the edge of the Peopleʼs Pueblos; just on the borderland of the Wilderness and the needs of the Pueblo; there in the Wilderness on the edge of the curiosity of the People who continue to laugh at all that these Monkey Boys do; the ones know as Kʼoy; the ones known as Spider Monkeys; the Ancient Ones o who were once formed and shaped from Tzʼite Trees. These Tree Being would be made from wood to be brought to life as the Wooden People of the Ancient Age of the People of Wood that lived out their fallen and failed lives during an Ancestral Era; during an Ancestral Sun that has come and gone yet left remnants and remembrances all along the way that are met up with today in the Forest of the Many Trees; Kʼi Cheʼ are their name.

And so they sprang up and off they went; up and away they climbed limb by limb through the trees to rise with ease ever so briskly straight up into the canopy of the many, many trees of the great forest of the Kʼicheʼ. Keyakatik xebʼe pa kʼechelaj.

“What are we going to do with you, you our beloved Grandmother? Because this time is the third time that we will try; this is the third chance to get it right, three out of four; before it will be four and then no more. That is all you have in store if you want to bring back your Boys who you care for more than any other Grandmother who has ever cared for her Boys; the Sons of your Sons, each one your Grandson. So this is it, one more chance to call them down and watch them dance. With this third dance it will be three chances; you have two more chances;

body:
two more songs; two more dances to come and then we are done,” said Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

And so they piped again; and so they drummed again, so that they sang again. And so they sang the song Junajpu Kʼoy again, and again they came in dancing.

The Song of Junajpu Kʼoy The Dance of Junajpu Kʼoy The Laughter and Fun of Junajpu Kʼoy

They came in dancing their dance; they began to dance their dance that they had already begun to dance that was a song. Their dance that was their song was Junajpu Kʼoy that they heard far, far away yet it called them back to where they had come from not so long ago. As they made their way back home dancing they just took it nice and slow knowing this was the way to go; moving back and forth; swaying to and fro; dancing their dance just like before. So they danced right up to door to then cross the threshold into Grandmotherʼs courtyard of Grandmotherʼs Great House; the Great House of the Great Mother, the Great Matriarch who her Grandsons and Sons danced for; for when they danced for her, the Grandmother; the Grandmother of their Ancestral Lineage of the Monkey Ancestors of Painters and Scribes; Musicians and Singers; Flautists and Drummers; Singers and Storytellers; Artists and Artisans.

All of whom were celebrated through their dancing the dance of Junajpu Kʼoy that was danced to entertain her, the Great Matriarch of the Hunters and Gatherers where Grandmother was entertained by her Boys; her Men by their dancing their dances for her; the Great Mother; the Great Grandmother; Matriarch of the Ixim Winaq. She who sat at the Center of the Horticultural World of settled and sedentary villages where men ventured out into the wilderness while the Women and Children; Old Women and Old Men stayed behind in their settled settlements to tend their planting and their sowing; to protect their flowering and fruiting.

body:
This is the story told here of the singing of the Song of Junajpu Kʼoy that called forth the dancing of the Dance of Junajpu Kʼoy that brought-on the Fun and brought-out the Laughter of Junajpu Kʼoy. The Song of Junajpu Kʼoy that caused the Dancers to dance the Dance of Junajpu Kʼoy; Dancers who were called upon by the singing of the Song Junajpu Kʼoy that caused the Fun and Laughter of the Song and Dance of Junajpu Kʼoy. Fun and Laughter that caused the Monkey Boys to leave once again humbled and humiliated by the laughter of the Great Mother and all the fun she had as the Old Woman who was the Grandmother that she truly was.

Ancestral Flute; Ancestral Drum Ancestral Rhythm; Ancestral Beat Ancestral Dance; Ancestral Song

Junajpu Kʼoy was the Ancestral Song that was the Ancestral Tune that was the Ancestral Dance that the First Pair of Twins danced when they came in dancing to the Ancestral Rhythm and Ancestral Beat of the Ancestral Song that the Second Set of Twins performed when they sang the song of Junajpu Kʼoy to the Ancestral Melody that was played on their Ancestral Flute and Ancestral Drum.

This was the ancestral flute that accompanied the ancestral drum that they played to the ancestral tune that the Younger Sons played out on their Ancestral Drum; the Second Couple of Sons; the Second Pair of Boys; the Second Set of Twins who brought forth Junajpu Kʼoy as the Ancestral Remembrance of their Ancient Ancestorsʼ Ancestral Lineage of Tree Ancestors; of Vine Ancestors; of Animal Ancestors; of Clay Ancestors; of Wooden Ancestors; of Reed Ancestors; of Birds Ancestors; of Shied-Warrior Ancestors; of Volcano Ancestors; of Earthquake Ancestors-Failed and Fallen; Flawed and Faulty; Defective and Damaged; Arrogant and Proud; One and All. These were those Ancient Ones known as the Divine Ancestors who were the Soul of the World; Anima Mundus; Mundus Imaginalis and its Imaginal Realm that was now brought to life through this Ancient Ancestral Performance of the Song and Dance; Fun and Laughter of Junajpu Kʼoy.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
All of which the Younger Sons piped and played; sung and drummed; the Younger Sons; the Second Twins who were these that were those; those who were they who were known and named: Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

It was they who invoked the enchanting dance of their Older Brothers with the ancient, ancient ancestral tune they played with their drum and flute while singing out their ancestorsʼ song known and named: Junajpu Kʼoy.

The song they played was the tune they piped; the tune they piped was the rhythm they drummed; the rhythm they drummed was the melody that was heard as their ancestorsʼ ancient ancestral song. This was the Original Ancient Ancestral Song of Junajpu Kʼoy; a song so charming that it captivated all those who heard it; a song so beguiling that it caused those who heard to heed its call by standing-up to then begin dancing along to the tantalizing tune of this enchanting song; for this was a deeply moving melody.

This was a song so soulful and sweet that one could not refrain from moving their feet upon hearing its beat. This was a tune whose rhythm and time were so sumptuous and sublime that it precipitated the electricity and heat of a thunderstorm. For one felt in ones bones like lightening that pulsed through oneʼs veins causing its tempo and beat to sprout forth through oneʼs hands and feet in soulful sorts of subtle ways.

Nevertheless it was the way the Boys played it that made Junajpu Kʼoy what it was. And what that was, was a call from above and below; a call from the Sky and Earth. A call from up above to dance in a spirited sort of transcendent joyful way; and, an invocation from down below to its tempo that moved oneʼs soul like the Moon animate pull on the Earth. Yet balanced by the transcendent spirit of the clear blue Sky which is why the dancing of the Boys was such a beautiful experience that brought forth an Ancient Ancestral sense of being ʼat Oneʼ with oneʼs Ancestors.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
It was ʼjustʼ by the way they played and piped it; sung and drummed; to bring it alive with the flute, drum, and voice of the Ancient Ones; the Ancient Ones who were the Nawal Sons of Nawal Fathers who became One when the Boys became their Fathers who had first played this Ancient Ancestral Song in its Original Way. For wasnʼt it the First Fathers who taught their Sons all they came to know before they descended down to Xibʼalbʼa? These Sons then were their Replacements-Kʼexel on the Face of the Earth and perhaps this is what one must know when telling this Ancient Ancestral Account of Boys who became their Fathers through a very refined education and the long ordeal of initiation that is revealed here in mythic metaphorical ways. Song and Dance of Junajpu Kʼoy is taught to Traditional Kʼicheʼ Musicians and Dancers right now and right here. Just as the Hero Twins, Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej played it out here.

This time their Grandmother controlled her laughter, truly she did. She did not laugh; she just did not do it; she didnʼt smile; she was determined to go through it; she wasnʼt going to laugh that was all there was to it.

The Old Woman just watched the dancers dance their dance without laughing at all for she was determined to excuse her laughter by not laughing out loud as she had done twice before.

The Monkey Boys: the Older Brothers; the Dancers of Junajpu Kʼoy climbed up upon the upper edge of the ledge that crowned the patio walls. That is when she noticed that the rims surrounding their eyes turned bright red, while their mouths frowned, sort of sadly, more or less pathetically; the whiskers stood-up straight on their fuzzy-faced muzzle and furry-faced eyes that looked like saucers; just like thatch grass stood their whiskers standing erect to give them a furry sort of fuzzy look that made them appear perpetually excited.

They looked as if there was nobody to groom them anymore; as if there was nobody who cared about the way they would appear when they danced; which now they looked like they were completely panicked and filled with fear.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
When Grandmother looked upon them with their scruffy unkempt faces the Old Woman just burst out laughing at once; she couldnʼt hold back anymore so she let out a great roar to then laugh and laugh and laugh as the Monkeys danced across the floor. And so the Old Woman was just filled with joy watching those Boys dance around the house with their long tails and bushy eyebrows; their big round eyes and fuzzy faces would make anyone smile to then start laughing until laughing was all there was. She was finished with trying to hold herself together so she just let herself enjoy the laughter provoked by these wild looking Boys who she had always kept spotless and groomed; elegant and neat; done-up and dapper; so very prim and proper as Artists and Artisans always appear.

Well that was certainly not how they looked now that they were off on their own out in the mountains where they had to make it on their own in the wilderness where they now made their home among all the other animals who they now joined looking for food wherever it could be found up in the treetops or down on the ground.

What else could the Old Woman do but laugh at these two for who they became through the nawal power of their Younger Brothers? The Old Woman she just laughed at the wild untamed way they now appeared; the rustic and unrefined way they now looked; now that they were wild animals without anyone to show care or concern for them out in forest with its many, many trees.

They no longer had any fear as they moved from limb to limb; tree to tree with their long tail and four feet that were like four hands with which they could climb in search of birds to have a bite of the fresh flesh theyʼd become so accustomed to. Monkey do eat meat as a sweet and salt treat and so they compete with the Birds for the tree tops where fruit and flowers; insects and grubs are found all around for those who can climb high in the treetops.

And so it was that their faces were no longer seen again by them because of their Grandmotherʼs laughter. Ma chi kʼu xil chi kiwach rumal utzeʼbʼal Atiʼt.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
But they tried anyway to call them with their flute, drum, and song because that was the way of the Boys, the Sons; those who were the Twins: Jun-Aj-Pu and Ix-Bʼalam-Kej. One Blowgun Boy and Little Jaguar Deer did what they did to make an example of the Monkey Twins: Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen.

“Just this time, just one more time, you our beloved Grandmother, we cautioned you, we advised you, we counseled you that we would only try four times. And this is the fourth time, the last chance, so do your best to pass this test to prevail over this ordeal to reveal you can overcome this trial.”

They took up their flutes to begin piping on their pipes as they played again on their flutes; but this time they didnʼt come back, the fourth time, straight-away they-their Older Brothers-went off into the forest and never came back again, they never returned home to their Grandmother.

It was there with their Grandmother that the Older Brothers had learned so much beside her ancestral fire that burned in her three stone hearth; the fire that warmed their hearts; the fire that sustained their souls; the fire that cooked their food. But that was all lost to them now as they entered the forest where they would be kept warm by the fur that now covered their bodies; the fur that now protected them from the cold.

This is when Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej spoke to their Grandmother: “Well we just did our best, you our Grandmother, Ix Qatiʼt at first our Older Brothers returned dancing to our playing and piping, drumming and singing; and then we tried to call them back again a fourth time but they did not return.

Donʼt be sad, we are here-Oj kʼolik, Oj iwiey, we, your grandsons, we your teeth-oj iwiey-we your replacements, we your descendants, we your remembrance who are here to make you happy; to make you content with our ways of warming your heart.” “We just love and care for our Mother and you, our Grandmother. Our Older Brothers will be well remembered for we shall remember them when we name them every time we play their song: Junajpu Kʼoy! So be it! Ta chuxoq!”

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
“Was it not they who became vain and arrogant; was it not they who acted as entitled lords to humble and humiliate their Younger Brothers? And are they not entitled and are they not named Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen because of this, as it is said; as it is spoken; as it is remembered by all,” said Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

They, Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen, were invoked by flute-playing flautists, song-singing singers, by the Ancient Ones, Ojer Winaq; the Ancestral People remembered them by playing and dancing out the ancient ancestral ways of their song: Junajpu Kʼoy.

But they never returned again to where they original came from; they just made their home in the forest on the mountainside as the reversal of their destiny called for. For it was they who just swung-up straight into the mountain as they moved about limb from limb; up and up they went on and on as they climbed as they made their way up and across the mountainside as they kept going higher and higher to be those who came to live at the very top of Jungle Wilderness where they live today as Lords of the Mountain. Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen were invoked by scribes and sculptors, painters and carvers, in ancient times. It was they who were transformed into animals; for they were transformed into the Spider Monkey-Kʼoy that is what became of them because they made themselves out to be greater than all the rest.

It was just their arrogant acts of arrogance; their self-aggrandizement that brought about their downfall and defeat; just like it did to the other proud and arrogant ones; and, as it always will to those who believe their essence shines as bright as the Sun in the light of Day; as luminous as the pearl-white-light of the Moon at Night.

The Older Brothers humbled and humiliated their Younger Brothers for a long, long time by holding them in their hearts as their servants-kʼeje wi kalibʼil chi kikʼux and not as their Brothers as it is said here in the Ojer Tzij.

Older Brothers-Younger Brothers;

body:
Noble Lords-Engendered Sons Which is to say the Older Brothers treated their Younger Brothers as if they were their subjects; they treated them as if they were their vassals known as Al, Kʼajol; Daughter, Son as the original invocation of the Popol Wuj speaks of the Saqil Al, Saqil Kʼajol; Precious Daughter, Precious Sons which is a fine refined way of speaking of the descendants; but this is not how these Pairs of Twins that were Couples of Twins treated one another and so those who acted as animals and by doing so caused suffering and pain; affliction and anguish were transformed into animals.

These animals are those that are perceived as they are seen which is as talented yet failed animal ancestors; animal ancestors who are seen as the First Ancestors-Nabʼey Winaq of the Ixim Winaq who will be formed and shaped from maize to become Maize Beings. But these Elder Brothers were formed and shaped from the flesh of animals for they ate the animals brought down from the mountains by the Hero Twins and so the flesh of their bodies did become animal flesh that was always hunted and eaten by the Ancient Ancestors of the Ixim Winaq as it is said here in mythic metaphorical ways.

It was just because of the humiliating treatment of the Younger Brothers by the Older Brothers that those Older Brothers disappeared-sachnaq chik; they were just lost to the remembrance of the lineages except as good example of what becomes of those who practice self-magnification. Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen became perfectly good examples of perfectly bad examples of speaking and acting. And so it was that they, Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen were reduced in rank, just lowered in status, lessened in stature like the Wooden People who were transformed into those who are known as the Spider Monkey-Kʼoy.

Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen Howler Monkey; Spider Monkeys

body:
This was when Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen disappeared from being the talented Artist and Artisans they were born to be from birth and through the training they received through their lineage of Artists and Artisans who and what they once were to become the fallen and failed kinds of Wild Animals that were there within them as their animal nature and essence that always lurks within beings who have no control over their appetite with its great power and potential to pull human being down into the lower forms and shapes of existence for humans and their struggle to be and become perfect and precious replacements of their Divine Ancestors; those known as the Nawal Winaq; the First Perfectly Formed and Shaped Beings of Maize. This is the story that tells of those First People of Maize and their first perfect and precious sacred way of being and becoming human on the Face of the Earth.

Those who are Spider Monkeys are found in the treetops of the Petén Jungle where they share the forest with the Mono Congo or Howler known as Bʼatzʼ. What a gift it is to spend time with these two species of Primate who make their homes near the Classic Maya Cities where Maya Day-keepers and Prayer-makers see them as their Ancient Ancestors who live on in the Ancient World of the Maya that is animated by the Maya Soul and Maya Spirit of those Ancient Beings who lived in this Sacred World for Thousands upon Thousands of Years of continuous and continual connection and communication with the Ancient Ancestors.

Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen, the First Sons of Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu were ʼcausedʼ to be lost; they were ʼcausedʼ to disappear in order to become in an instant that which they had called forth into existence as the animals they always acted and spoke before their perceived rivals; their imagined adversaries their Younger Brother. And that is how they became the animals that they always had been and continue to become as this very mischievous and ruinous; injurious and dangerous Kʼoy.

body:
For truly they became ʼanimalsʼ and their descendants can be seen swinging and heard howling through the jungle forest as the Kʼoy who Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen were transformed into being; they just became those known as the Spider Monkey that is who and what they came to be. These Two Boys molded and modeled themselves into perfectly fine example for those who wanted to become Wild Animals just like them: e chikop xeʼuxik.

New Domestic Life of the Domesticated Twins: Ixim Acha New Life of Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej as Men of Maize: Hombres de Maíz

It was then that they made themselves at home. As flautists, they just played their flutes; as singers, they just sang their songs as they began to play-out; live-out the new ways of their new domestic lives as the replacements-kʼexel of Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen as Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej entered where their Older Brothers had been not so long ago.

They-JunAjPu, IxBʼalamKej-accomplished great things; so that in no time at all they demonstrated; as they revealed; as they expressed their nawal essence- xekʼojeʼik that was the nawal condition-kʼojeʼik that was their true nature while living there with their Grandmother and Mother who now showed them the care and concern that manifest as deep respect and high regard, even favor, for them as their Boys, their Sons, ri Kʼajolabʼ.

They eagerly began showing all they could do as they revealed their many capacities and capabilities by working while playing flute and singing songs there before their Grandmother and-pu their Mother; chuwach katiʼt, chuwach pu kichuch.

Jun AjPu; AjPuj; AjPuuh Nawal Puff of Power; Nawal Puff of Life;

Nawal Puff of Change; Nawal Puff of Transformation

Again this use of ʼpuʼ for the conjunction ʼandʼ is also a stupendous play on this nawal ʼpuffʼ as a ʼshamanic breath of magical exaltation-expiration of life energy. This is the way ʼPrayer-Makers and Day-Keepersʼ transform the ʼenergyʼ of whatever space-time dimension they are working on as healers and diviners who cleansers and clearers of the ʼdead or stagnantʼ energy of a situation or condition that requires cleansing and clearing.

body:
There are many situations in the Popol Wuj that call out to be magically transformed through the shamanic blast of breath through the use of the ʼpuffʼ of breath. This is the ʼpuuhʼ that is an expulsion of ʼlife forceʼ that exists in the expiration of ʼair or aireʼ that transforms the energy of existence or being . This can be ʼpuffingʼ away at the ʼshamanic blowgunʼ of Jun Junajpu and Junajpu who must ʼtake-downʼ an undesirable being or essence or condition or nature or situation as an ʼact of blowing awayʼ an enemy or rival or adversary like Wuqubʼ Kaqixʼ or the ʼblowingʼ on the Birds on the Path with Kabʼraqan and Jun Bʼatz, Jun Chowen.

There are many situations in shamanism that are not desired so they are first ʼblown backʼ as that which is not wanted to then invoke, in order to petition, in order to call in and receive that which is desired through this ritual act of ancestral transformation. This is how AjPuj or AjPuuh depends up his of ʼblowing out an expirationʼ to cleanse and clear away negative or toxic types of energy; or, the opposite in which one is ʼblowing a blessingʼ over a person, place, or situation. This ʼshamanic breathʼ is also used in healing to cleanse and invigorate a person who is ill.

Puuh or Puuj is the ancestral exaltation leading to change and transformation that is the work and way of AjPu or AjPuj or AjPuuh. This is also a primordial type of strong aspiration that is propelled out as an ensouled intention of breath as life force. This is extremely important to Day-Keeping and Prayer-Making who must use their ancestral powers of shamanic incantation and invocation of ancestral enchantment that are ʼbreathed outʼ the exhalation of breathe. I highly recommend ʼplayingʼ with it to get a real ʼsenseʼ of the inherent power of this aspiration.

Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej began to know what it felt like to be settled down-e ramaqʼelal into a domestic life of sowing and tending the milpa now that their days of living as the servants-alabʼil were over.

Milpa of Maize; ri Abʼix Their Axe, their Hoe, their Blowgun; Kikaj, Kimixkina, Kiwubʼ

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
The first work that they wished to perform was to walk out to where they would begin working in ʼla milpa-ri abʼixʼ that was their family cornfield that was their Milpa of Maize-ri Abʼix.

“We are just-xa going to go work the Maize in the Milpa you who are our Grandmother, and you who are our Mother,” they said.

Xa kojabʼixik, Ix QaTiʼt, Ix pu QaChuch. “Donʼt be sad, we are here; we, your Grandsons; we, the replacements of our Older Brothers,” said Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej. So then it was that each one of them took up their axe-ki-kaj as they took up their hoe-ki-mixkina to carry them on their shoulder-ki-xokem before heading out to the mountainside, each one of them shouldering their blowgun-kiwubʼ xkitelej.

They left their house after giving instructions to their Grandmother as to when she was to bring them their sustenance: “When the Sun is straight overhead come bring us our Mid-day meal, you, our Grandmother,” they said. “Utz bʼa la, you my Grandsons-Ix Weʼy-you my Teeth, you my Replacements,” she said then, their Grandmother.

When they arrived there at their milpa they took up their hoe and sunk it in the ground where it began to do their work hoeing the ground; the work of theirs was to use the hoe to ʼcut-upʼ the earth; to form row after row to sow their seed to grow their milpa.

The work of their hoe was to sow the seed to grow the maize; all of which was theirs to do with their hoe that the Boys asked their hoe to do on its own; they asked the hoe to do the work that was the work of a hoeʼs to do which was to sow row after row of seed so that their maize would grow and grow in their milpa.

And just like that their hoe knew just what a good hoe must know; which was where to go and what to do when it came time to do what it was asked to do. And what their hoe was asked to do was to sow their seed to grow their maize.

And so their hoe formed row after row of Milpa so the Boys could sow row after row of Maize that would grow and grow as row upon row of Milpa that would grow and grow into perfectly formed heads of Maize; Maize that would grow and grow into perfectly formed rows of Milpa; rows of Milpa that were shaped into perfectly formed rows of growing canes and heads of Maize.

Their hoes would form perfectly formed rows of canes of Maize that would grow and grow in row after row of perfectly grown heads of maize that would grow and grow in row after row into a perfectly formed canes with healthy heads of Maize that would multiply and grow in the Milpa of perfectly shaped heads of Maize with perfectly formed seeds filling out the big beautiful mazorcas of Maize.

Their hoe worked all by itself; it knew just what it had to do; just as it knew where it had to go to do what it had to do; which was to clear the field of brambles and brush to sow row after row of Maize; Maize that would grow and grow into perfectly shaped Mazorcas in perfectly shaped rows of Milpa.

body:
This was the work of their hoe that worked all alone doing all that it was asked to do; which was to work all alone sowing row after row for the Boys who knew this work was theirs to do; to do all alone with their hoe that they put to work on its own to do the work that was theirs to do but that they gave to their hoe and asked it to do what was their work to do. It wasnʼt only their hoe that was asked to work all alone; it wasnʼt just their hoe that was asked to do what it had to do as a hoe that was asked to work all alone on its own. No, it was not just the hoe who worked all alone because their axe too worked as it was asked to do when it was asked to work all alone; when it was asked to clear the land of the trees and vines for the hoeing of row after row of Milpa; to sow the seed to grow the Maize; for the sowing of the seed and the growing of the Maize was done by the work of their hoe. Their hoe that hoed and hoed row after row of Milpa of Mazorcas of Maize that were perfect heads of Maize that grew and multiplied; to then multiply and grow into full heads of Maize. This was the Milpa they would sow that was the Milpa they would grow when it came time to grow row after row of Maize in their Milpa that would grow full with great big beautiful Mazorcas of Maize that would grow to fruition in la Milpa.

And so their hoe and the axe were asked to work on their own when they were asked to work all alone. Those Boys just sunk their axe in the trunk of a tree for the axe to begin clearing away the forest of its trees and vines; when axe cleared away the brush and brambles of the forest then their axe quickly turned to cutting up its branches and limbs of the trees into perfect pieces of firewood.

body:
Before long, the trees and vines were cleared down to the ground; this is where the forest once stood and where the milpa would soon be standing; standing where it would be sown by the Boys to be grown in row after row of maize that would grow and grow in the milpa; it was just the Boys who worked the milpa on their own with their axe and hoe that worked all alone. Perfectly stacked rows of firewood were what had become of the forest that just one hard-working axe had chopped-down and cut-up all by itself as the hard- working axe of the Boys.

The axe that completed its work by working completely on its own; all alone; by itself; that was the way of their axe; the way of axe of the Boys who worked the Earth with their axe and hoe yet were hunters by nature their names said so: JunAjPu; IxBʼalamKej; Ancient One Hunter and He-She of the Little Jaguar-Deer.

And as for the hoe, well low and behold it just plowed up a whole big expanse of forest; immense was the area of thorny brush that this one hoe cleared away in less than a day and completely alone as it works all by itself to clear the way for a massive milpa of maize.

Truly vast was the piece of land that this one hoe turned over as it plowed the ground as was asked to do; on the Small Mountain-Chʼuti Juyubʼ; on the Big Mountain-Nima Juyubʼ as well.

It was all brought to fruition by the work of their hoe and axe that did the work that was theirs to do. What was theirs to do was to sow row after row of milpa that would grow and grow as perfect canes of maize upon which would grow full heads of maize to gather together a great harvest of maize to feed those who needed to be fed.
