body:
This was theirs to do or at least that was what they thought to be true until something happened that would cause a little small someone to tell them what they knew was truly theirs to do in a life where they had to be true to who they were born to be in a world where destiny is a very particular thing that each and everyone must bring into being by coming to know that which is oneʼs own. Or else we end up missing the show in which we were created for to be and become the leading actor of our own show and its main performance that was written just for us to reveal for all to know and all to see as that which is played out as our destiny.

This is where the Boys are confused because they want to warm the heart to heal the ʼbluesʼ of their Grandmother for the loss of the Boys who danced to Junajpu Kʼoy and can no longer work their One Head of Maize in the Milpa like before. So Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej think they must fill-in for the loss but this is no way to live life in a Sacred World where each and everyone has a destiny that they alone must fulfill like the Axe and Hoe of the Boys who know just where to go in order to do just exactly what they must do. But the Axe and Hoe are not the destiny of Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej and this they must find out in their own way which they do; which they most certainly do.

And so it was that these Two Boys gave their instructions to an animal-jun chikop Dove-Xmukur-Paloma was her name.

They placed Dove-Xmukur-Paloma on the trunk of a tree and then Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej said: “Just watch for our Grandmother when she comes to give us our food, just cry out when she comes up the trail, so we can grab-hold of our hoe and our axe so it looks like weʼve been working.”

body:
“Utz bʼa la,” said then the Dove, la Paloma-xechaʼ kʼu ri Xmukur. Meanwhile they were just out hunting with their blowguns-xa wubʼanik. Hunting birds with their blowguns is what they knew. This was what they knew; this was the only thing these two knew what to do that was truly theirs to do; it wasnʼt true that they were out working the milpa, as they said they were going to do when they left the house in the morning to work in their milpa. So this then was when Ixmuqur-Dove-Paloma cried out as a sign; as a signal that Grandmother was coming. They ran back to their milpa where they were working: one grabbed hold of the hoe and one grabbed hold of the axe.

They just bundled up their heads like real workers; each one bound their head with their headscarf-chipis kiwi.

One of them ʼintentionally-xloqʼ-deliberatelyʼ covered his hands with earth; the other one dirtied his face with dust just like a true worker of the milpa would do; like one who truly worked the milpa-qitzij abʼixom-un milpero de verdad. The other one ʼintentionally-xloqʼ-deliberatelyʼ threw woodchips all over his head like a true woodchopper would do.

This is how they wanted to present themselves to their Grandmother who was the ancestral authority when it came to the growing of their milpa. But really Grandmother will be the One who deifies Maize by growing Four Divine Varieties of Maize in ʼher Houseʼ so realize there is a great deal going on here. One of them is that these Two are Maize Deities; they are Maize Lords so this deceptive play of the Tricksters here must have been a lot of fun for the Maya since trying to deceive Grandmother is impossible: Grandmother-IxMuqane is the Great Mother of Maize she is a major sort of Supreme Deities or Kabʼawil but in the most significant kind of way for she is the Great Matriarch of the Maize People. You should know this so you can understand Grandmother is the Dove; she is Ixmuqur!

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
And so it was that when Grandmother arrived they were seen as humble workers of the milpa; one a hard-working field hand or ʼmozoʼ with his hoe in hand and the other a hard-working woodchopper with his axe in hand. This then is how they were seen by their Grandmother who climbed up the mountainside where they were working so hard to bring them their mid-day meal.

This was when they sat and ate their mid-day meal with their Grandmother. They ate the food their Grandmother carried-up the mountainside to bringing to them where they worked.

They just sat and rested to eat together alongside their work in the milpa where they worked with their axe and worked with their hoe that they had used to do the work of clearing the forest for the growing of their milpa that they would soon sow to then tend when it sprouted out and began to grow maize in the milpa.

For truly, the milpa of theirs that was to be sown to then be grown like a true milpa was the milpa that they would sow like a true milpa but first they had to prepare that milpa of theirs with their axe and hoe.

But it wasnʼt true; they werenʼt really working in the forest clearing there where their milpa would be sown and grown by their axe and hoe that worked all by themselves; absolutely alone even though their Grandmother brought them their food as if they were doing their work completely on their own.

They just made it look like they were working with the hoe and axe when they were just doing what they liked most and were born to do with names like Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej; One Blowgun Boy and Little Jaguar Deer; these two were natural born hunters who would come to see the milpa as a lure to entice the animals that they would come to hunt at night; their milpa being the place from which their sacred sustenance was harvested. The milpa of the Maya is truly an enchanted place where nobody goes unless it is theirs to tend and protect.

The Popol Wuj just jumps ahead after the meal and the afternoon work so donʼt be surprised that they are coming home in the evening after a long days work.

As soon as they arrived back home they said: “Truly we are just all tired out, you our Grandmother, Ix Qatiʼt!”

body:
Then they ʼintentionallyʼ just sort of ʼdeliberatelyʼ rubbed their muscles down while stretching their legs and arms there before their Grandmother. Those Boys just feigned the soreness and exhaustion of true workers. Right there in front of their Grandmother they made a show of all the work they had done in the milpa that day with their hoe and axe.

Their axe and hoe that knew just what to do and just where to go; their hoe and axe they asked to work not too fast and not to slow to hoe the milpa row by row for the seed to be sown where the maize would be grown by the axe and hoe that worked entirely alone; by themselves; all on their own.

The following morning the Boys returned to where theyʼd worked the day before in their milpa-pa kabʼix; only now all the trees; all the vines were left standing-up straight-kʼisyakatajinaq chik ronojel cheʼ, kʼaʼm.

The trees, the vines were bound-back together, twisted-up tighter than before so that the forest was sealed-off by a knot of thorny bushes; bristling brambles.

“Who has pulled this over on us?” they asked then.

“Apachinaq kojmichʼowik?” Xechaʼ kʼut.

This was the doing of all of those known as:

Small Animals; Chʼuti Chikop, Big Animals; Nima Chikop Who were named:

Puma; Koj Jaguar; Bʼalam Deer; Kiej Rabbit; Umul Fox; Yak Coyote; Utiw Jabali; Aq Coati; Sis Small Birds; Chʼuti Tzʼikin Big Birds; Nima Tzʼikin These are the ones who did it; in just one night they did it all by rising-up together in the darkness to then incite the forest to rise-up.

In one night under the cover of darkness the Birds and Animals summonsed the Trees and Vines to stand-up again there in the forest where the limbs of its trees and the arms of its vines had always been the dwelling place of the Animal People; the Ancient Ones, the Ancestral Residence of the Forest; their Original Habitat; their Natural Abode; the Dwelling Place of all many Birds and Animals who had been given their Mountain Places and Living Spaces in Canyon Country for their House and Home; the Forested Wilderness that had always been their place to multiply and grow.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
It was in just one night that they did it; they brought the forest back to life when they raised it up once more in order to leave it standing as it stood before. So once all over again the Boys began working their milpa with their hoe that knew just what to do; their hoe that knew just where to go in order to perform their work as it had been done before to prepare the earth for where their milpa would be sown; for where their maize would be grown. For a second time their axe knew where to go and what to do to level the trees; to then cut-up the branches and clear-away the brush; tear-up the roots; and clean-up the mess by burying the twigs along with the leaves before helping the hoe clear away the weeds to prepare for the seeds to be sown in the rows that were hoed in the milpa so the maize could be grown were the axe had been left to do its work on its own; by itself; all alone.

Cutting and Chopping Clearing and Cleaning

And this is exactly what they did once more on their own so that their axe and hoe could complete the work of the Boys with their hard-working tools that were content to do what was theirs to do all by themselves; for they knew what they knew which means they knew what to do and just where to go to prepare the milpa by clearing the land and hoeing the rows to sow the maize where it would come to grow as fine canes of maize where beautiful heads would show the face of the First Ancestor whose skull-headed seed was planted in the milpa long, long ago.

This was the Boys second attempt to clear the land of trees and vines for the sowing of their seed in row upon row maize sown in the milpa that soon would be sprouting and growing as the result of their work that was their cutting and chopping; clearing and cleaning; hoeing the rows for the sowing of seed that was a sure way of showing their nawal way of knowing just what to do and just what say when it came to working the land to transform the Face of the Earth for the Sowing and Dawning of Maize Peopleʼs Nawal Way of Life of axing and hoeing for the seeding and the sowing of the sprouting and growing of their precious Milpa of Maize.

body:
Then the Boys gathered together their thought-kinaʼoj their genius-kinaʼoj their insight-kinaʼoj in order to take council with one another there where the trees had been cut-down by their axe on its own; where the earth had been chopped-up to be cleared-off and cleaned-up with their hoe that had worked all alone.

When they gathered together their knowledge there where they cut-down the tree and cut-up the earth Ta xkʼam chi kʼu kinaʼoj chiriʼ pa qʼatoj cheʼ pa qʼupuj puch…

This was when they brought together their thoughts-naʼoj…their genius-naʼoj…their insights-naʼoj where they cut-down the trees and where they cut-open the earth…This is a metaphor that speaks of ʼheart sacrificeʼ as the reciprocal payment of the human debt for cutting- chopping down the trees and cutting-chopping open the earth in very metaphorical, mythic sorts of ways…pure Ancestral Thought…pure Ancestral Genius…pure Ancestral Insight…pure Ojer Naʼoj…as one might say today in a genius sort of thoughtful kind of insightful type of way… These genius phrases speak of the Maize Peopleʼs sacrifice Mountain-Plain with its trees and vines of the forest and the soil that is the flesh of the Face of the Earth. This sacrifice of the Trees and Vine; Bushes and Brambles; Fields of Flowers and Open Highlands of Thatch Grass; Earth and Land; Ground and Soil creates the ʼGreat Debtʼ of the ʼMaize Peopleʼ that must be paid back to the Ukʼuʼx Kaj; Ukʼuʼx Ulew through human sacrifice where and in which the human head is ʼchopped-offʼ through ritual decapitation and the chest ʼcut-openʼ to then the heart ʼcut-outʼ to be fed to the ʼheart of the fireʼ as the beating rubberball of human heart sacrifice. So realize there is much more going on here than what appears by a superficial reading of this magic metaphorical mythic text.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
Remember IxKikʼs ʼheart sacrificeʼ and the way her heart as a ʼround thingʼ is turned over in the hands of the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa. This is the ʼround rubberballʼ of the rubber-like ʼmuscleʼ of the human heart that continues to beat after being ʼextractedʼ from the chest ʼcave- ityʼ to be placed on the sacrificial fire that burns bright on the altar of sacrifice when its fire is ʼstirred-upʼ to getting nice and hot. Kʼate chi kʼut xkitikʼibʼa chik abʼixik. Xawi xubʼan chi ribʼ ulew rukʼ qʼatoj cheʼ. Ta xkʼam chi kʼu kinaʼoj chiriʼ pa qʼatoj cheʼ; pa qʼupuj pu…This is what is spoken of above as the ʼcutting-offʼ and the ʼcutting-throughʼ the head and the chest…the trees and the earth…the trunk of the trees and ribs of the earth…These are the same words used when Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame sacrifice Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu who are dismembered and decapitated by the Lords of Sacrifice; Lords of Death; Lords of Xibʼalbʼa.

These verbs ʼqʼatojʼ and ʼqʼupujʼ were used back then and now here again to bring out these signs, symbols, and significations of the reciprocal relationship between the ʼgift and debtʼ being paid just right through human sacrifice as the ʼflesh and bonesʼ of a Human and ʼsoil and stonesʼ of the Earth are ʼcut-off-qʼatoj-dismemberʼ and ʼcut-into-qʼupuj-plowʼ but it is also used by Jun Kame-One Death when he says: ʼxkiqaqʼupuj-we will cut your lineage off and xqʼat ujolom ri Jun Junajpu-they decapitated Jun Junajpu.

This metaphorical play on these very particular kinds of specific verbs is just so very rich so that I want to ʼbring them outʼ here so that you receive an understanding of the sense and sentiment of these words: ʼqʼatoj and qʼupujʼ.

These words are often associated with the verb for sacrifice and the place of sacrifice ʼpusik-pus-pusbʼalʼ which of course brings out another play on the name of the Maize Deity who is also a Lord of Sacrifice; Lord of Death with is body marks of One Death-Jun Kame and Lord One Sacrifice: Jun AjPus!

Junajpu is hard at work here sacrificing the forest by cutting the trees-qʼatoj cheʼ and cuts open the earth-qʼupuj ulew for the sowing of the Maize and its growing in the Milpa.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
So then it was there in the forest that the Boys began working their milpa; where the Boys stood with their hoe to cut-open the earth to prepare the ground and its rich soil for the sowing of their seed.

This was where the forest had been cleared and cleaned by their axe that had cut-down the vines and trees to clear away the brush and brambles; bushes and weeds; limbs and leaves to ready the milpa for the sowing of its seeds.

This then was when they brought together their thoughts to contemplate their ideas and consult their imagination to reveal their nawal genius as they celebrated council with one another to consider what was required from them to bring about the sowing of their maize in their planting of the milpa.

“We must just sleep here in our milpa to keep watch through the night; this way we will catch them by surprise to see what they are doing in our milpa in the middle of the night,” said the Boys when they gathered together to talk over their thoughts and ideas.

“We must remain vigilant and stay right here through the night to surprise those who did what they did and most certainly will continue to do all that they do. We might just bury ourselves undercover to capture them in the middle of the night when they gather together to do what they do right here in the darkness of night,” said the Boys as they made their plans. “Really, we must remain awake through the night right out here in our milpa so we can catch those who are pulling one over on us. We might just hide right here where we can snatch them to catch them to capture them; so we can seize them to stop them from doing what they did again,” said Boys as they revealed their complete comprehension of what needed to be done in order to do what they were called to do.

This is what they said when they gathered together their thoughts; when they took council with one another; when they came to an accord there in the forest; there before their Grandmotherʼs milpa.

This then was when they gathered up their axe and hoe; when they shouldered their blowgun to return home where they would talk it all over again with their Grandmother and Mother.

body:
It was then that they arrived home. Xeʼopon chi kʼut chi ja. “Who is pulling one over on us, you our beloved Grandmother? The thatch- grass has grown right back and the forest once again stands where the earth had been left so perfectly prepared-cleared and cleaned-for the sowing of our seed. We found our milpa completely grown back with tall pajón-bunch grass-nima kʼim chik and a great big forest-nima kʼecheʼlaj when we arrived there just a short while ago, you our Grandmother, Ix Qatiʼt,” they said then to their Grandmother and Mother.

“So then, we shall just be going. We will sleep there on the mountain because it is just no good what they are doing to us,” they said; the Boys, the Sons, the Twins: Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

Then they readied themselves, they bundled themselves up with protective cotton cloak-xebʼatzʼonik; they covered themselves with a light suit of cotton- batting not knowing who or what they would be combating in the middle of the night.

So then they went to where they had cut down the trees of the forest to clear it for their milpa; it was there that they hid themselves-xematzeje wi; it was there where they buried themselves in the damp earth there-e muqumuxinaq chire.

This is when the animals gathered together as one single council; as just one-xa jun council of Forest Animals; they sat on the ground together so that all the Small Animals, all the Big Animals; Chʼuti Chikop; Nima Chikop came together as Just One: Xa Jun.

And so this then was when they came together in the very Heart of the Night; when the Heart of the Night stood straight-up over head-tikʼil Ukʼuʼx Aqʼabʼ.

In the Heart of the Night is where the Animals were now gathered; when they gathered together as ʼjust oneʼ council of Animals that stood as one to speak out about what mattered to them most: the Animals of the Forest.

And so it was that they spoke straight to the point as one voice when they gathered together in the middle of the night as Just One: Xa Jun.

This then is the language they spoke when they spoke their language- kichʼabʼal at Midnight, “Yaklin Cheʼ, Yaklin Kʼaʼm, Rise-up Trees, Rise-up Vines…Yaklin Cheʼ, Yaklin Kʼaʼm, Rise-up Trees, Rise-up Vines.”

body:
This is what they said, this is what they sung, as a beguiling incantation to enchant the trees and vines of the Forest by those who had been given this place of the trees and vines; the Forest where they were bestowed their sleeping places among the canyons and ravines where the sustenance was always there to be found as long as there were no people around to cut the trees and vines to the ground.

The Big Animals and Small Animals entered there together in order to form a line to bring forth the forest that had always been theirs.

They lined up under the trees, under the vines in the forest, in the brush and brambles; this is when they appeared, when they showed their faces; then and there they just called upon the trees as they called upon the vines of the forest with their enchanting incantation spoken together as one invocation there in the middle of the night: “Yaklin Cheʼ, Yaklin Kʼaʼm, Rise-up Trees, Rise-up Vines…Yaklin Cheʼ, Yaklin Kʼaʼm, Rise-up Trees, Rise-up Vines.”

This is when the Animals appeared from beneath the trees and vines; this is when they showed their faces so the Boys could see who was there when they came out in the forest in the middle of the night. The first ones were the Puma-Koj; the Jaguar-Bʼalam. The Boys tried to catch them but they didnʼt give themselves up easily, they just bound away with their long tails waving up and all about them; there was no way to catch them because they moved so fast the Boys never touched them.

Then came the Deer-Kej; the Rabbit-Umul it was they who would appear next. The Boys almost got them when each one almost caught one by their tail; but the tail of the Deer just popped off in the grasp brother; just as the tail of the Rabbit was lopped off by the clasp of the other. And so it was the Deer and Rabbit who gave up their tails to those who tried catching them to only end-up snatching away their tails.

The popped off tail of the Deer and the lopped tail of the Rabbit were snatched away by the Boys leaving their tails bobbed to this day.

body:
This is how Deer and Rabbit look today with their chopped off and cropped off tails so there is no way to catch them or snatch them away when theyʼre eating maize in the milpa. This is said to have been a fair exchange for their losing their tail when they went bounding and bouncing away to escape the grasp of the Boys. The animals didnʼt give themselves up easily; Fox-Yak, Coyote-Utiw, Jabali- Aq, Coati-Sis ran right in front of the Boys; so that Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej never even touched them.

This just burned up their hearts; the truth was that they could not catch a single one of them; for the Animals slipped right through the Boys grasp to avoid being caught in the Boys clasp when they tried catching the Animals by snatching their tail but it was to no avail because those Animals just ran right passed those Two Boys who had hid out there to find out what the Animals were doing out there in the Boysʼ Milpa that was the Animalsʼ Forest. But there was one more there; the last one who was there was all alone; on his own; known to all as the Last One of the Road: Xambʼeʼ.

There is that which is yours in Life Sowing the Seed; Growing the Maize Tending the Milpa Is Not Yours in Life

These are the Forest Animals who the Boys thought would be easy to catch by grabbing hold of their tail. ʼButʼ they were not easy to catch for it was not easy to grab and then grasp their tail. Animals are fast so itʼs impossible to grasp their tail in order to capture them for real. The reason for the speed of the Animal and why they never gave themselves up to the People is because they showed the Ancient Ones known as the Former; Shaper where they could find their Yellow Maize; White Maize to form and shape the First Four Fathers of the Maize People.

White Maize; Yellow Maize will be revealed to the Former, the Shaper; Molder, Maker; in exchange for the Big Animals; Small Animals being given their portion of Maize in the Milpa that is sown to be grown in the Milpa that once was the Forest of the Animal People.

body:
This will be revealed at the ʼendʼ of this ʼtaleʼ that speaks of the Boys quest to find that which was truly theirs in life; their destiny which is the story that is told here of the Animals who knew what was theirs in life to bring to completion. The Animals know what was theirs to bring to fruition in life; a life in which one needed to know what was oneʼs to do to then just go out and do it. And this the Boys will find out soon enough to then carry it with them up the road to begin doing what is theirs to do in life.

So letʼs get on with it; letʼs get on down the line to tell that tail-end of this ancient ancestral tale that tells of tails and their getting burnt in the end! Burnt in the end to reveal that which is oneʼs life that is never revealed to one without entering the fire to feel the pain and suffering of ordeal; ordeal that is the essence of initiation; and, this story is a story that in many ways begins here with the initiation of the Hero Twins; Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej when they find out what is theirs in life to bring to fruition; when they find out what their destiny is; which, is not working in the Milpa for their Mother and Grandmother.

Working in the Milpa is not theirs in life; but, there is what is theirs in life and they must find it. And they must find it now!

Uxambʼe chik; the Last of the Road Chʼo; the Ratoncito; the Mouse Trickster arrives to Reapportion Sustenance

So then came one more, he was the last one: uxambʼe chik. Just bouncing, just bounding down the road he came, as he came hopping and bopping along the road not seeing where he had to go; not seeing who he was about to run into as he came jumping down the road.

This is how Mouse-Chʼo came when they saw him coming hopping and bopping along-xa katzotzotik ta xpetik towards the First and Second Son. It was they who then grabbed him by the throat as they grasped him by the neck there behind his head they just wanted to strangle him to finish him off; to finish him off right then and there.

body:
Kʼate kʼut xkiqʼatej, xkise kʼut pa qul ri chʼo kʼate puch xkichapo, xkiyotej puch chirij uwi xraj kibʼiyo. They tightened their grip around his throat thinking that by strangling him he would talk but then they realized that was no way to go about getting what they wanted so they burnt his tail over the fire to be told all he had to tell.

Why were the Big Animals, Small Animals there beseeching the Trees and Vines to rise- up; to rise-up again out of the place where they had cleared the Forest to clean it for the Milpa for the sowing of their Maize?

But the Mouse said nothing; keeping what he knew within him not wanting to reveal what he knew so well was theirs to have; so he kept quiet not saying a word until he got what was his in life in exchange for that which was theirs; and, what was theirs was their destiny; and, their destiny was to fall in their Fathersʼ footsteps by becoming their Father and Grandfatherʼs Sons instead of the remaining the Sons of the Mother and Grandsons of their Grandmother. Popol Wuj is a mythic metaphor that tells of tells of Ritual Initiation while telling the Myth of the Maize People through which the ʼLife of the Hero Twinsʼ is the Mythic Lifecycle of the Lords of Maize being born in the Underworld of Xibʼalbʼa to rise-up within the body of their Mother and then grow on the Face of the Earth until now when they will become the Replacements-Kʼexel of their Fathers the Maize Lords to live out their Destiny as Noble Lords.

This then was when the Boys brought Mouse-Chʼo over to the fire to then burn his tail over their flames and that is why the Mouse has no hair on his tail.

Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej grabbed him hard and held him so tight that his little black eyes bulged out of his head. And so it is said that it was because of the way the Boys, the Sons, the Twins throttled Mouse that is eyes almost popped out of his head. This then was when he began crying out; this then was when he began calling out as best he could while they held him down as hard as they could!

“I should not die because of you! Ma ta kinkamik iwumal! I should not die because of you! Ma ta kinkamik iwumal!” “What is yours in life is other than your working in the Milpa! Mawi are ipatan ri abʼixik! Your destiny is not that of a Milpero; not you two; this is not your destiny; but there is that which is yours; Kʼo iwe; Kʼo iwe-There is what is yours to live. There is that which is yours!” Cried the Mouse when he prepared to tell the Boys that which was theirs; that which their destiny to live was. “This working the milpa is not for you; this is not what is yours in life; this is not your burden to bear. There is your destiny that you must live!” Said the Mouse.

“Ma to kinkamik iwumal! Mawi are ipatan ri abʼixik. Kʼo iwe!”Xchaʼ riʼ Chʼo. “I can tell you what is yours! Donʼt kill me; I will tell you what is yours in life; and what is yours is that which I carry within me here; so donʼt finish me off; for I should not die because of you! Ma ta kinkamik iwumal!”

“The Milpa is not yours to bring to fruition; the Milpa is not your burden to bear; the Milpa is not yours but there is what is yours; and, that which is yours is what I bear within me,” said Mouse.

La Milpa El Destino del Pueblo de Maíz The Destiny of the People of Maize “La Milpa: its four precious corners; its four perfect sides; its jade seeds; its ancient roots; its resplendent sprouts; its green leaves; its sweet canes; its golden heads; its shimmering tresses; its flowering tassels; its buzzing bees; its whispering wasps these are not yours to bring to fruition-mawi are ipatan ri abʼixik; chopping with the axe in the Forest; hacking with the hoe in la Milpa; working its perfectly aligned rows; hoeing row after row of maize that grow in milpa is not the burden you were born to bear in life; but there is what is yours and its is right over there.”

“Working the Milpa-Abʼixik is not yours to fulfill; your ʼgeniusʼ is not tending and protecting la Milpa; it is not yours to do, for it is not your calling; it is not your life; not your truth! Yet, there is that which is yours; there is yours to come true; it is over there; over there is what is yours; your destiny, your sacred burden to bear; your ancestral calling to heed; there is your ancestral vocation; the ʼgeniusʼ that is you,” said the Mouse-ri Chʼo-el Ratoncito.

“Where is it; this that is ours? What is it; that which is ours? ¿Apa kʼo wi qe? Tell us now!-Chabʼij na kʼut! Speak then; tell us now; what is it; where can we find that which is ours that can be found!” asked the Boys to the Mouse.

The Destiny that is Ours to Live There is that which is Yours-E kʼo Iwumal What is that which is oneʼs destiny? What is oneʼs calling on the Face of the Earth?

The question raised here is of the greatest importance to the Kʼicheʼ Maya who like all of Mesoamerica will follow the Divinatory Calendar know as the Sacred Count of Days from which they will be provided guidance and protection in all they do and wherever they go. The question for humanity is how do we human beings know what is ours in life; and, how do we know what to do once we find what is ours?

body:
The Boys, the Twins find out what is theirs by catching ʼa Ratʼ that is ʼa Mouseʼ who they must give up everything that is of valuable to the Maya which is their sacred sustenance in exchange for what they want and need in life to survive. Popol Wuj is founded in this primordial exchange between Divinity and Humanity: What do we need to survive and what are we willing to give in exchange to receive what we must have to survive? This is the character and condition of survival just as it is essence and nature of sacrifice: what is our sacred sustenance and what must we sacrifice to attain it in abundance? The Boys who are the Engendered Sons of Jun Junajpu receive a boon; a great gift from the Mouse known as Chʼo for the Knowledge of Destiny that they receive from him that is a ʼlife and deathʼ question of first, survival; and, then prosperity. The Mouse provides the Boys Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej with what they want but the cost of this exchange that is made for this Knowledge of Destiny is outrageously expensive indeed. For the Boys are willing to sacrifice all the sources of human sustenance-maize, beans, cacao, pepitoria, chili, and all Mouse can find to chew up-as the payment they give in exchange for what they receive from Choʼ the Mouse. Mouse is he who tells the Boys not only what their destiny is but where to get it while they must once again use their nawal-genius to deceive their Grandmother and Mother; IxMuqane and IxKikʼ in exchange for the gift of their destiny.

The gift of their destiny is the Ball-play Gear; the Ball-playing Regalia that you know so well but have not seen because it remains where it was left knotted up in the ʼrafters-utum jaʼ of Grandmotherʼs House. How will they enter Grandmotherʼs House to cut the knot of their Fathersʼ inheritance so their ʼRubber-ball and Ball-playing Equipment can fall down to where the Boys can grab it and then take it to then begin playing ball with it. This is what is theirs in life; this is their destiny to play-out in life.

Yet, there is that which is yours; there is your dream to come true; it is over there; over there is what is yours; there is your ancestral essence-kʼojeʼik, the ʼgeniusʼ that is yours; your ancestral presence-kʼojeʼik,” said the Mouse-ri Chʼo-el Ratoncito.

“Where is it; this that is ours? ¿Apa kʼo wi qe? What is it; where is it; this that is ours?” asked the Boys who now begged the Mouse to answer their question.

“Tell us then now!-Chabʼij na kʼut! Speak then; say then what is ours; tell us then where this that is ours can be found!” pleaded the Boys who began to feel a certain sort of care and concern for their new friend and ally: the Mouse-ri Chʼo. “Well let up on me a little bit then because the truth of my word is within me; release me and I will tell you what I have to say; just give me a little bit of that which is mine; give me a little bit of that which is my sustenance!” said Mouse. “So then, we will give you what is yours when you tell what you have to say,” they said to him. “Kʼate chiqayaʼo awechaʼ, chabʼij na,” xuchaʼxik. “Utz bʼa la! Very well then! All that is your Fathersʼ, all those things that belong to them; those who are your Fathers; those whose names are Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu; those who died in Xibʼalbʼa; their ball-game equipment, their ball-playing gear; all of those things that are theirs, are yours; all that they left behind is yours; this is that which is yours: the Ball-playing Regalia and their Rubberball. That which was theirs is that which is yours; their Ballgame Equipment is what stayed right here, it remains where they left it, hanging down from where they left it tied up in the rafters of their house-pa utum ja:

Their wooden yokes: kibʼate for ʼbeating-bʼaʼ the ball on your hip Their arm guards: kipachqʼabʼ to protect your arms from the ball Their rubber ball: kikikʼ from the rubber sap they tapped from their trees

“Just donʼt show them to your Grandmother; it was ʼjust-xaʼ because of them that your Fathers died,” said the Mouse-ri Chʼo-el Ratoncito. “Can it be true all that you say?” asked the Boys to the Mouse, chi re Chʼo.

They felt such great contentment knowing that there was something that was theirs in life left behind by their Fathers; their hearts-kikʼux where made sweet when they received the news, the word, the truth about the rubberball-utzijel kikʼ.

It was time then that they gave Mouse what was his; the sustenance that would always sustain Mouse-rechaʼ Chʼo the food that was given to him is what it continues to be: Maize-Ixim White-seeds of Chilacayote squash-Sakil Chili-Ik Bean-Kinaqʼ Pataxte-Peq Cacao, Kakaw

“This then is what is yours-Are kʼut awech ri! All of the food that ends up in the rubbish is yours to discover. All of this that is hidden away and poorly stored is yours to enjoy; just eat it up! Chakʼuxu! Chew it up! Grind it up!” This is what was said to ri Chʼo, the Mouse by Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
“Utz bʼa la, Ix Kʼajolabʼ; Well alright Boys, I just wonder what should be said if your Grandmother sees me? What should I say?” he asked then, ri Chʼo. And so they explained to him what they would do to retrieve what was theirs from where it was now hanging in the rafters of Grandmotherʼs house. “Donʼt lose heart Ratoncito mio, you donʼt have to worry about that my Little Mousito, we will be there, we know how to speak to her; we know just what to say. Straight-away we will leave you there in the corner of the house from where you will make your way to where the ballgame equipment is hanging.” “There we will see you clearly through the hole that opens up into the rafters of the house-the tabanco-utum ja-as it is known, as it is named; utum ja; en el tabanco de la casa; in the rafters of the house. Only we will be looking down in our soup to see you up above,” they said to the Mouse when they gave him his instructions, when they took council with one-an-other when they brought forth their plan, the plan that was the idea of Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej. And so they went walking down the mountain from where they had once wished to sow the seed of their Grandmother and Motherʼs milpa. Now they were returning home with a different sense of who they were and what was theirs in life.

When the Sun stood straight overhead was when they arrived where they now returned-kʼi kʼu tikʼil qʼiij xeʼoponik.

For it was exactly at ʼMid-Dayʼ when they arrived; the Sun was ʼstandingʼ directly above when they returned. The Mouse-Ri Chʼo could not be seen when they carried him in to Grandmotherʼs house when they entered to have their mid- day meal of chili-water soup.

One Son entered straight into the house-jun ri yakalik xok pa ja;

One Son entered at the corner of the house-jun kʼu xok xikin ja where he quickly set Mouse-Chʼo up under the rafters of Grandmothersʼ house.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
This was when they asked Grandmother for their food, their ground chili- water soup-qʼutum ik: “Perhaps you might grind-up a bite for us to eat, we would just like to have a little ground chili-water soup; a nice warm broth of ground roasted red chili-qʼutum ik-you, our Grandmother- Ix Qatiʼt,” they said then there when they spoke to their Grandmother there in her kitchen; there in her house where she slept to tend the embers of her fire that never went out there in her Three Hearth Stone fireplace. And so then she fixed them their meal, just a bite to eat. One bowl of ground chili broth was ʼplantedʼ before them there as their food that was ʼplacedʼ in a bowl before them to eat.

Only they pulled a fast one on their Grandmother and Mother. They emptied the clay water jug-qʼebʼal-tinajaʼ by evaporating it away with their nawal powers of evaporation-kitzajisaj kʼu jaʼ pa qʼebʼal.

The Boys Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej use their powers of evaporation to evaporated the water out of Grandmotherʼs big round clay water jug: qʼebʼal.

Clay Water Jug or Qʼebʼal known as a ʼTinajaʼ from here on out in this story of Grandmotherʼs Clay Water Jug-Qʼebʼal that will be spoken of as a ʼTinajaʼ which we see Yax Bʼalam pouring over his Father the Maize Deity-Jun Ixim on the Resurrection Plate of the Boston Fine Arts Museum.

“Truly our mouths are dry from our great thirst, Grandmother. Perhaps you might bring us something to drink,” they said to their Grandmother. “Wee! Fine,” she said then, when she left.

So then they went on eating. But it wasnʼt true that they were hungry. Just deception alone was their doing; just veiling the vision of their Grandmother was their way of making this way of deception of theirs; they just wanted to hide what they were doing there.

It was then that they saw the Mouse in their ground-chili-water soup-qʼutum ik. He was there curled around the rubberball; the rubberball that was hanging down from up above in the house: xekel wi puwi ja.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
They saw this in their ground chili water soup that Grandmother ʼplantedʼ before them; they looked up above into the tabanco when they looked down below in their bowl of soup. This then is when they sent for the strong Little Black Gnat that was a Powerful Little Fly that bores holes in the side of earthen wall before the rains arrive; this is the one known as Xaʼn who they sent on an errand of theirs; Xaʼn is just a living sign of nature that tells us when the rains are on their way.

Now this Xaʼn is like an Us who is a Tiny Black Gnat that leaves a swollen round mark and a little spot of blood that is a ʼsignʼ one has been bitten hard to have their blood suckled from oneʼs flesh. Xaʼn is a word that also signifies transgression as in somebody doing someone else wrong or even harm.

The Boys just sent Xaʼn to over to where Grandmother was beside the River, by the waterside-chi Jaʼ and there it was that Xaʼn began drilling out the ʼfaceʼ of Grandmotherʼs tinaja-qʼebʼal from which water now sprang forth from all the little holes that Xan bored out with his or her tiny drill of snout. It was out from these tiny perforation that water began to pour out of Grandmotherʼs tinaja-qʼebʼal that couldnʼt hold water anymore. This was the clean drinking water she had gathered up from the spring that sprung from the side of the river. This was the water collected by Grandmother to calm the thirst of her Boys.

The Old Woman tried but she just couldnʼt do it; she couldnʼt close-up all the holes that the Xaʼn bored into her tinaja from which water now poured forth from the terracotta face of her clay water jug known as an ʼollaʼ known as ʼtinajaʼ spoken of here as Grandmotherʼs tinaja: qʼebʼal. This then was when the Boys spoke so all could hear what they had to say:

“Whatever could have happened to our Grandmother? Where is she? What could she be doing? We are just desperate for a bit of water. We will soon be finished off by our thirst,” they said.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
This is when they directed their speech directly towards their Mother. This was when they sent their Mother out for a little bit of water to quench their burning thirst that came from their Chili-Water Soup-Qʼutum Ikʼ; there was nothing else they could do they just had to send her out for their water, so truly parched were their mouths now.

It was then that the Mouse gnawed away at the twisted rope from which hung the rubberball and all that hung bundled together with it up in the rafters of Grandmothers House-pa utum ja.

It wasnʼt long they had wait before it all took a fall to where they were waiting to catch it down below; this ancestral bundle of their Fathersʼ ball-game equipment and rubberball that hung down from up above in the tabanco-pa utum ja.

This was when the Chʼo cut through the rope so it didnʼt make a sound when it fell down to the ground where the Boys were there to receive it there beneath the rafters of the house;

The wooden waist yoke: ri bʼate The jaguar-skin arm guards: pachqʼabʼ The deer skins: ri tzʼum for protection Immediately then, they gathered it all together; they just gathered it from where it fell to the floor. Then they went off to where they hid their bundle beside the road; there on the Road to the Ballcourt; there on the road to the Ballcourt- Burial Grounds-Jom; ubʼeal Jom.

The Road to the Ballcourt is where they hid what had been their Fathers and was now theirs with which to play the ballgame which was theirs to play with their rubberball which was theirs to play ball with for now they had it all: their ballgame equipment and their rubberball. For truly all that was hanging up there in the rafters of the house was now theirs to ball on their ballcourt; and, what was theirs was what had been their Fathers.

Quickly then did they arrive to where their Grandmother was beside the water-chi yaʼ.

Their Grandmother-Atiʼt and Mother-Chuch were there beside the river where they were doing their best to seal the face of each one-jujun-of their tinajas- qʼebʼal or clay water pots specially made for carrying water.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
They arrived beside the river, each one-jujun with a blowgun. This is when they addressed their Grandmother and Mother.

“What is going on? We ran-out of patience; truly, our hearts tired of the wait, so we came to see what may have happened to you here beside the river; here beside the water-chi ya,” they said. Grandmother said: “Just look at the face of my clay tinaja, there is no way to seal it; drip, drop; drip, drop; there is no way to make it stop,” said Grandmother. But the Boys, the Sons, they sealed it up immediately; instantly they closed up all the tiny holes on the face of Grandmotherʼs clay tinaja her terracotta water jug with which she carried all her water.

And together they returned home, this time it was they, the Boys, who walked before their Grandmother; the Grandsons just led the way back home.

In this way the rubberball ended up with them, for it now ʼremainedʼ with them to ʼstayʼ in their possession; this ball of theirs that was their Fathersʼ rubberball. And so it was that the Boys, the Sons were left with their Fathersʼ rubberball playing ball and their ball-playing equipment; their protection and adornment, their headdress, gloves, yoke, and skins.

Utum Jaʼ; Utum Ja: the Dew from Dusk to Dawn; Horizontal Rain of the Warm Wet Nights of the Dry Season

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
The Hero Twins are now coming into their own since they now know who they are as the Sons of Fathers; Sons of Fathers who know what is theirs to do in life as Noble Lords who are Noble Ballplayers of the Rubberball Game that is the inheritance they have received from their Father and Uncle known collectively in the Popol Wuj as their Fathers: Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu. Popol Wuj is the ancestral expression of the Nature and Culture through the mythic metaphor of the Lifecycle of Maize. And now this Myth of Maize tells us that the rains are coming and the Maize Deities mouths are dry. This is the time of year when cultural expression of myth reveals the dry state of the Natural World when the sprouts of maize are shooting up out of the earth by being ʼembraced by the warmth of the Sunʼ and ʼpulled up by the growing powers of the Moonʼ at a time of the lifecycle when the Maize Twinsʼ dry mouths thirst for water.

Popol Wuj is a very clever mythopoetic literary expression in which the life of the Hero Twins across the mythic landscape: the Milpa of IxMuqane; the House of IxMuqane, the Forest of the Kʼicheʼ; the Ballcourt of Jun Junajpu and soon on the Ballcourt of Xibʼalbʼa known as the Sacrificial Ballcourt of Ballcourt Sacrifice known as Pusbʼal Chaaj. We are about to enter Xibʼalbʼa and then onto their Sacrificial Ballcourt-Pusbʼal Chaaj where this Myth of the Maize Lords will be played out on this ʼBallcourt of Sacrificeʼ as a life and death ordeal to see who wins: Life or Death. Can Death be killed is the question Popol Wuj answers in a most decisive way to reveal the Maya People as an Eternal People who will always return: cycle after cycle; Sun after Sun; Age after Age; Era after Era; Harvest after Harvest as the Sacred Narrative of Sowing and Dawning; Dawning and Sowing; Round and Round; the Eternal Return of Life in its victory over Death.

body: The ʼBall-game Regaliaʼ are what will dress the Maize Lords in order to ʼgo to battleʼ against the Lords of Death so think about the various lists of the ʼBall-game Equipmentʼ and how each element of the ʼBall-game Gearʼ signifies a body part of the Maize Lord. Consider how this Noble Ball-game Regalia express the power and authority of the Hero Twins who wear their ancestral accoutrements as the natural aspects of Maize Deities: ornate headdress as maize tassel; mask and headscarf as the ancestral face of the mazorca; deer skins-leaves and cane; jaguar arm guards-leaves; wooden yoke-nodes of the cane; jade-bead necklaces and jade-bead bracelets as the resplendent essence of life. The Maize Lord will be dressed and embellished with these ornaments to embody and ensoul the Noble Lord of Maize as he who was born in the Underworld to the Moon Maiden-Moon Mother who is the Moon Goddess who is the Mother Goddess of Night who give birth to Divine Twins Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej who will immolate themselves on the sacrificial pyre in ritual sacrifice to free their ancestral soul and spirit to ascend into the Sky as the Sun and the Moon. So realize there are many levels of this myth that are coming to fruition right here so please take your time to read this deep interpretation of this Translation of Popol Wuj or skip ahead if that is what you would rather do because there will be plenty of interpretive explication that will be provided to sustain this sacred textʼs need of interpretation. After all, the Maya were initiated into their positions of warriors and ballplayers; scribes and painters; singers and musicians; sculptors and carvers so why wouldnʼt the reader of the Popol Wuj be initiated into their understanding of Popol Wuj through interpretive revelations such as that which is presented below; interpretation in which natural science and cultural expression are brought together to reveal the deep meaning and profound significance found here in the Ancient Word of Popol Wuj.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body: Dry Mouth-Chaqij Chiʼ Dew Water-Utum Jaʼ Tzuy Wa-Sacred Secret Speech The maize sprouts that come up and out of the ʼapparentlyʼ dry earth at the beginning of the growing season are watered from the night time dew known as utum jaʼ or water gathered inside the ʼtwisted conical cupʼ created by the natural twisting of the sprouting leaves of corn plants. This is what the Popol Wuj is telling us here through this masterful mythic metaphor of Hero Twins as two young sprouts of maize and their hot dry mouths that thirsts for a drink of refreshing water. Let us discover how this comes forth as the Boys call out to the Grandmother and Mother for water to quench their thirst because of the red-hot heat of their red-hot chili water soup-qʼutum ik-ground dried red chili that has left them parched with thirst.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body: This is mythic language is formed and shaped from secret sort of sacred speech that is the metaphorical language of mythic image and mythic metaphor that is known to the Maya as the language of Tzuy-Wa or Suywa or Suyua. Tzuy-Wa is known as the Original Olmeca-Xicalanca language which is beheld as the ʼoriginal ancient languageʼ of the Gulf Coast of Mexico where the Original Maize People come from known as the Gourd Head People or Tzuy-Wa or Xicalanca which in the Nahuatl language signifies Gourd Head a name that is derived from Tzuy- Gourd and Wa-Head which is the Gourd of Sustenance as in Tzuy-Gourd and Wa-Sustenance which is the Divine Sustenance-Saq Waʼim that is drank in its original form of taking maize as sustenance which is by drinking maize gruel or atole from a gourd bowl-tzel or gourd drinking vessel or tzuy. You known this name Tzuy-Wa as being part of the original place of natural abundance and plenty beside the reeds and rushes of lakes and estuary known as Tollan Tzuy-Wa this place is found on the Gulf Coast of Campeche known as Xicalanca where xicalli signifies gourd and Xicalanca being the Place of the Gourds or House of Gourds known to the Maya as Tzuy-Wa. These Olmeca-Xicalanca are the Original Rubber People who are the Gourd People taking us back to the origins of the Mesoamerican World and its Mesoamerican Cosmos. Tzuy-Wa was explained to me by a Kʼicheʼ Day-keeper as the Divine Knowledge of the Changing-Transforming Way of Life, Death, and Rebirth on the Face of the Earth. This is the knowledge of the Nawales; the wisdom of the Nawales; the language of the Nawales; the ways of transformative power of los Nawales. And since I brought it up I might as well say something important here about the way Translation and Interpretation of Popol Wuj have been performed by the Maya before me which is to say they are so much more creative and free to make connections and associations that the Academy would find impossible.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
Maya Shamans and Prayer-Makers who are Interpreters of Dreams allow themselves much richer and much more playful in their down to earth kinds of interpretations and translations founded in Ancient Ancestral Indigenous Knowledge and wide-open word play through ʼfree associationʼ. Free association that would never be accepted by the Academia yet revealing a profound sense of knowing of the playful sense of Nawal ways of being and becoming in life. This is the kind of Nawal knowledge and understanding that is much more true to Indigenous Ways of Being and Becoming in the world that is always going to be much more interesting than the Academic Translations and Interpretation of Popol Wuj. What can I say? It seems ridiculous to have to say it while at the same time wanting to be truthful about the vast difference between Academic Translations and Interpretations and true Indigenous Translation and Interpretation of these Kʼicheʼ Maya Prayer-makers who feel and sense the nature and essence of their sacred Maya Kʼicheʼ Language that forms and shapes this the Kʼicheʼ Mayaʼs Ancient Ancestral Book of Nawales who are Ancient Ones in whose footsteps enter the pages of this Sacred Book formed and shaped from secret sacred speech.

This work here attempts to bridge these two worlds while acknowledging that I will never feel ʼfreeʼ enough to bring out the subtle plays of the ʼNawal Speechʼ of invocation and enchantment I have explored with Kʼicheʼ Maya Day-keepers and Prayer-makers who are Seers and Diviners; Healers and Herbalist; Matchmakers and Mid-wives; Bone-setters and Sweat-Bath specialist. These Mother-Fathers of the Ancient Word never fail to shock me to the core by the connections they make that express an understanding of sacred language and ancestral knowledge that is a completely different sort of Indigenous expression of myth and metaphor; incantation and enchant through the Ancient Word-Ojer Tzij. Anyway, do realize how rich the Ancient Word of Popol Wuj and how this work here is just barely touching the surface as profound as it might appear to be to those who are just coming to the Popol Wuj for the first time.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body: And this magnificent play on words is a play I would have never known had I not been out walking early one morning to accidentally meet up with an elderly old Maya Man of Maize who was up early on the mountainside tending his milpa. It was the Old Man-Bartolo who mentioned the utum jaʼ in his milpa and kind of laughing about how wet the soil beneath each of the sprouts was sopping wet since the ʼtwisted cup of leaves or utum jaʼ had gathered dew water that had collected through a very wet night to leave his milpa deeply watered by the ʼhorizontal rainʼ that falls as dew throughout the dry season on the mountainside of the exceedingly wet countryside surrounding Lake Atitlan and the forests that surround it. This dew falls heavy from dusk to well after dawn using the leaves of the maize plant as a water catchment system of such genius that leaves one awed by the Maize Plant and it natural nawal sort of genius as a living being who is alive and filled ancestral soul as the Maya People who tend the maize in the milpa as their very own flesh and bone as the sacred sustenance that maize is for the Maya and Maize who need one another like Night needs Day and the Sun the Moon…balance and harmony is the essence of the story told here in the Popol Wuj. What is most remarkable about this place where we are in the Ancient Word of the Ancestral Account is that now we have arrived at the time of year from late January to May when heavy dew falls like horizontal rain to provide the water that falls out of the sky all through the night from dusk to dawn unless there is el Norte and then the Lord of Death has taken the form of a very deadly drying wind. But if there is dew falling then it falls heavy and deep across the Face of the Earth. Like sap that drips from the Moon Goddess IxKikʼ, this watery essence that falls is that which was once known as ʼitzʼ drops as the heavy dew that drenches the milpa from sunset to sunrise during the first two moons of the lifecycle of maize in the highlands and lowlands of the Kʼicheʼ. As in the word pitz that may come from: pa itz or from its essence or pitzʼ as in the prana-like;

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
Heart of the Sea was experienced in the water that ʼevaporatedʼ into the sky during the day that was seen as ʼitzʼ and the ʼutum jaʼʼ or water that came from the vault of the sky or rafters of the ʼgreat houseʼ as the sky-earth was once conceived by the Maya. This Great House is IxMuqaneʼs House which is to say IxMuqane as Grandmother is the Great Matriarch of the Sky-Earth; Lake-Sea from which all life comes and returns to go ʼround and roundʼ through the rebirth of all being. But the Sky-Earth has energy moving up and down; over and under in the Sky and on the Earth.

The Popol Wuj is playing with this with the Hero Twins evaporating the water out of Grandmotherʼs Clay Water Pot or Qʼebʼal to then have the water fall back to earth and onto the maize growing in the milpa to fill the utum ja with ʼitzʼ or ʼessenceʼ that is dew and nurturing kinds of nourishing energy. This is important. The Maya are explain the Cosmos to us through their Sacred Narrative of Maize so we best to our best to listen to the text as best we can which hasnʼt been to great if you are to read past translations and interpretation that are usually literal and then mistaken on top of it. Sorry to say this but it simply the way it is. Popol Wuj studies are ahead of us not behind us; we just begun to understand the intricacies of this text. So there is the evaporating powers of the Hero Twins that cause their Mother and Grandmotherʼs Clay Tinajas to empty and there is the evaporating powers of the Sun that pull the water up into the Diurnal Sky while there is the Nocturnal forces of the Moon that cause that evaporated water to be pulled back down to Earth. The Maya Highlands is a very wet place to spend the night especially after a hot day in the Dry Season with a warm Full Moon night without wind. This then is when the Face of the Earth is literally drenched with dew water. Our text is telling us this as it tells of the horizontal rain produced by the dew watering the newly sprouted maize in la Milpa.

body:
Utum Ja is named here as the ʼtabancoʼ or ʼraftersʼ of the house of Jun Junajpu, the home of Grandmother who has not been called IxMuqane since IxKikʼ gathered up the One Big Net of Maize. That is interesting in and of its self. Grandmother becomes a Mythic Archetype who loses all of her individual personality for she becomes the Ancestral Archetype and Mythic Figure of the Old Woman-Atiʼt and the Grandmother-Atiʼt. But we are in her Sons House or Ja that is not called a House or Ochoch which is a structure where a Ja is a Home but also a House as in Nima Ja as in a Great House of a Kʼicheʼ Lineage.

But utum jaʼ is also the leafy ʼcupʼ that the maize plant forms with its long broad leaves that come ʼtwistingʼ up and out of the center of this highly ʼcreativeʼ and rather ʼingeniousʼ maize plant. This spiraling sort of twist cup that is shaped by the leaves of maize gathers the dew that falls on the rough feeling leaves that have tiny hair-follicles or ismal or ʼpeach fuzzʼ that catch the dew that collects upon the furry kind of hairy sort of fuzzy surface of the maize leaves to then have that water begin to drip and then drop and then run to then pour down inside the maize plant that creates a true ʼflowʼ of water into ʼutum jaʼ or ʼgathering cup of dew waterʼ of the maize plant.

This is the inside of Grandmotherʼs House so Grandmotherʼs World is that of Maize making her house an image of the maize plant where the ʼball-playing gearʼ are taken down from the tabanco or rafters or utum ja so they can be worn by the Boys who are about to embody and ensoul the life-ways of the Maize for they are Maize Lords who will be ʼdressedʼ by beautiful naked maidens just as is shown in Classic Maya Images of the Maize Lords being ʼdressedʼ nubile women. This is going to happen later on in the telling of Popol Wuj.

body: Meantime, you are getting the idea of what is going on here because eventually the Maize Lords will dance just as the Maize Dances in the Sun in July and August when the Milpa transforms into a very fertile and sexy place. The bees are buzzing and birds are chirping as the cornflowers of tassels come to life just as the long golden hair of the corn silk is ripe for fertilization. You get the idea right: the mythic metaphor of the life of the Maize Lords is played out be the Mythic Figures; Mythic Archetypes that perform the Ancient Account of Popol Wuj. My wish for this translation is that the coming generations may experience the perfection of their ancestorʼs noble ancestry experienced in every single word that are all metaphors for those objects, acts, beings, and events spoken of here in the sacred secret speech and metaphorical-symbolic language of Popol Wuj. Words just like utum ja that are always translated away into ideas like ʼthe hole that opens up into the rafters of the houseʼ or the ʼlashings of the houseʼ or ʼthe garret of the houseʼ which is to say the translation destroys any possibility of ʼentering the wordʼ of the Popol Wuj in any decolonized sort of Indigenous way of reading this Sacred Book of Ancient Ancestral Advice. So that translation and interpretation dries up the soulful word-play and to evaporate any type of indigenous understanding just like the harsh power of the sun-light at mid-day so is the literal scientific kind of rational-materialist-empiricist understanding of Popol Wuj. The Lords of Death are very much alive and they walk around with titles of academic power to rule and reign over the Indigenous Mythopoetics of Popol Wuj. But let is not dwell on the negative any longer since the admonishment has been delivered as needed as we can move on.

body: This word-play of ʼpu tum jaʼ or ʼpa utum jaʼ will continue with the soup that is asked as the sustenance of the Boys; Sons who ask to be fed by their Mother, Grandmother. The ask for an exceedingly simple yet highly signifying soup that is known as ʼqʼutum ikʼ which is ʼground- up chili water soupʼ that is a very ʼhotʼ red soup that is chili that is toasted to dark reds and browns to look like a bowl of embers so if you are Maya you understand somebody just turned up the heat at this time of the year in late March and early April when it gets so very hot in the middle of the day when they ask for their soup when the Sun is stand straight over head. But that is another matter completely or is it. Because it is down into their chili water soup that they will look up into the utum ja or opening into the rafters of the house, the opening into the sky; this reflection of the above and below of the evaporating water and the falling dew create the movement through this passage of the Popol Wuj; a passage throughout which one feels the water flowing forth from the tinaja or qʼebʼal of Grandmother and Mother and the evaporation going up into the sky that will fall with the dew. The sun of the chili water soup and the falling of the ʼnoble ball-playing regaliaʼ in the form of the green leaves of maize as in the skins and jade jewelry of bracelets and necklaces and the yoke that are the all important ʼjoints in the canes of maizeʼ and the headdress that is the corn tassel known as zute or tzʼutuj and on and on it goes. So one must follow the mythic images to find out what they are saying to us who have entered the Ancient Word of the Popol Wuj.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
Utum Ja or Utum Jaʼ, the opening up into the conical roof of thatched covered houses of the Highland Maya mirrors the conical cup of the maize plants as inverse images of one another as the Sky reflects the Earth; as the Earth reflects the Sky to form and shape the Sky-Earth where water flows from the outer darkness to fill the inner spaces of these little leaf cups of gathered water, utum ja. IxKikʼ comes from a family of gatherers and so it is here sons will gatherer water within themselves as maize plants who survive to thrive from gathered water from the Night Sky that is planted straight up above ʼas ifʼ a star that was planted like the Red-Giant Arcturus that is there at the very center of the Night-Sky.. And here is the twist you have been waiting for: tumaj is the verb that signifies the action of twisting, tumin is to twist chord and tumaj is to ʼtwistʼ and that is exactly how the maize leaves twist themselves into a cup, ʼutum jaʼ translated as ʼits twist of waterʼ and that my friends is how a translation of ancient ancestral mythic language becomes a mystical journey that simply leaves one not only mystified by the beauty of the Mayaʼs Ancient Word but misty eyed because of the deep hope one has for the Maya to renovate their world and culture by forming something new out of something that is very, very old.

Utum ja, a twist indeed. Utum ja, the place in the Sky-Rafters of Grandmotherʼs house. Utum ja from where Jun Junajpuʼs noble ball-playing gear will enable them to go to war with the Lords of Death, Lords of the Underworld, Lords of Xibʼalbʼa.

This is where the Boys will dance their rivals towards defeat and fiery sacrifice by dancing them into the sacrificial stone oven of sacrifice seen as the very Heart of the Sun there in the very Heart of the Sky: Ukʼuʼx Kaj. Pu tum ja is the opening through which the ball playing equipment of the rubber-ball-players falls to the Boys, the Sons who will take it up to give form and shape to those who will defeat and destroy the Lords of Death.

body:
This is the ball playing gear that will Boys to defeat the Lords of Death; Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame who will be defeated by the Boys, the Sons, who will be ʼdressed in precious jade and turquoise adornment of their Fathersʼ so that these Twin Maize Beings will take up the eternal return on the path of the Sun, on the road of the Dawn; at the time of the Sowing and Dawning.

The jade jewelry, the turquoise embellishment accentuated by the translucent green emeralds are the finery that will be worn by the Maize Deity; those who are Dancers known here as Jun Ajpu Ixbʼalamkej once known as Jun Ajaw, Yax Bʼalam the sons of Jun Ixim the Maize Lord who as you know is spoken here as Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu. Out of the utum ja the Boys, the Sons must bring down their fathersʼ ball playing regalia as the insignia that will provide them with magical ancestral protection just as the maize plants growing in the milpa will gain more and more protection against the dryness by growing more and more leaf with more and more follicles that gather more and more water to fill their utum ja, their spiral twisted cups of water to drink in the Night Sky through gathering power or pulling power of the Moon Maiden, Moon Mother IxKikʼ.

This dressing the Sons with their Fathersʼ cotton armor is much, much more than our limited understanding of the Maya Civilization enables us to comprehend. But what we do know we are on the path that will led us deeper and deeper into the twisting motion that this art of translation and interpretation we are participating through our forming, shaping of this translation.

That is very much like the dressing of the Maize Deity by twisting its leaves over one another in Twin leaves that shadow one another as they complement one another as the maize plant that is a maize being who comes up and out of the Earth to reach into the Sky spiraling up oh so invisibly to then flower with a tassel, to then fruit with two heads; two mazorcas of maize as in the two Boys, two Sons, the Twins of the Mother Moon IxKikʼ whose lunar breast are suckled by them as ʼdewʼ that falls throughout the outer dark of night.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body: This is the water gathered by the maize plant in its little twisted cup of twinning leaves; water that becomes the flesh of the body of the maize plant that becomes the flesh of the mazorca filled with fleshy kernels, with fatty grains, with oily seeds; rich seeds that become the sacred sustenance that feeds the fleshy bodies of the Ixim Winaq; Ixim Winaq who drink their rich thick fleshy sustenance from skull-headed gourds known Tzuy Wa: Gourd Head, Gourd Sustenance. Wa is a word that speaks of the food, the sustenance made of ground white maize or saq ixim or saqijal; and ixim is always translated as maize, sometimes as sustenance but now we know it means that which feeds the infant through their taking their mothersʼ breast to then suckle their life-giving; life-receiving sustenance. Ixim then is that word formed from ʼIx- signifying origin or from that which it originates; and, ʼIm-the teat on the breast that is suckled by the hungry infant, Ix-Origin and Im-Nipple to create the word and the world of Ixim, that which is suckled from the breast, that which is suckled from the nipple to create Ixim- Sustenance. So that the Ixim Winaq are those People-Winaq who take their Sustenance-Ixim that is the sacred sustenance suckled from the breast of oneʼs mother in a world where all creatures must search for their sacred sustenance so that they might live life on the Face of the Earth. Popol Wuj is the Mayaʼs Sacred Book of Sacred Sustenance that tells of the miracle of maize being sown beneath the earth to rise-up as a most magnificent plant among a great community of plants known as a Milpa. The Maize People then are the individual plants while the Milpa is the Pueblo that lives as one great community of beautiful and valuable ancestral beings who feed and are fed for all of time; from now to the end of eternity or as the Ojer Tzij rech ri Popol Wuj says: Saqil Amaqil.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body: Feed to be fed; feed and be fed; feed to feed others who canʼt feed themselves and so goes the profound struggle to provide a meaningful translation that will feed its readers so they may be fed to then feed others with knowledge and understanding; wisdom and beauty. This is the way of the Maya, this is the way of this mythic metaphor of maize found in these two words and the many ideas that are gathered from these words that create a metaphor spoken of as utum ja. Utum Ja or Utum Jaʼ the little cup of doubling, twinning, pairing, and kenning maize leaves that twist their way up the cane to assure they collaborate and complement the feeding of themselves as maize plant that they embody as the leaves of maize that participate with the entire plant to feed and water itself in the natural life-cycle of sustain and be sustained by sustenance without end. In this case the maize plant seeks to feed itself by catching perfect portions of sustenance from the Night Sky from the dew that the maize plant takes in from dusk to dawn. This is because the maize plant can be seen and understood as a water and nutrition catchment system that collects more and more water and nutrition the more it grows and grows to end up delivering large quantities of sustenance that is filled with perfect quantities of nutrients that are pulled out of the Night Sky with the dew.

body:
Now add that idea to ʼsmall mouth or small openingsʼ known as ʼstomataʼ that are found on the leaves of the Maize Plant that open and close as ʼminiature mouthsʼ to regulate the intake and outtake of water and nutrition of all plant life. These stomata are opened and closed by sound like the singing of ʼsongbirdsʼ at dusk and dawn to ʼfeedʼ the maize plant in perfectly balanced sorts of natural ways of feeding maize in the milpa with its sustenance. Natural ways of providing sustenance to the maize growing in the milpa in which nutrients are taken into the plant in the form of essential minerals and trace elements like amino acids that are gathered in the water particles of the dew that fall from the Night Sky to be deposited on the leaf of the maize plants growing in the milpa. This is what is going on with this sacred story of sacred sustenance that tells us a very detailed story of Sacred Sustenance that in many ways we are only beginning to understand.

The Maya are telling their story of transforming movements of Nature in a most creative way but it is up us in our age translate and interpret their words and images on their terms and in their context so we come know the Ixim Winaq a bit more like they knew and known themselves. The Ixim Winaq, those grateful people who know the origin of their essence, maize, as well as the sacred story that tells of the essence of the Mayaʼs origins: Popol Wuj.

Popol Wuj, sacred sustenance of the soul no matter who you are, and so here it is to be suckled as the very motherʼs milk to fed oneʼs forming and shaping in creative process of feeding the Nawal Winaq coming into being through being fed through the images and archetypes, myth and metaphor that come to life in the miracle known as the imagination of matter. Come, it is time to get a move on, down the road to the ballcourt that leads to another invitation to play the rubberball game known as chaaj in Xibʼalbʼa on the Ballcourt of Sacrifice known as chaaj with the rubberball that is known as chaaj but also kikʼ which means blood-kikʼ or sap-kikʼ or rubber-kikʼ or moon-ikʼ or chili-ik.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
Fatherʼs Ball-Court Fatherʼs Ball-Game Fatherʼs Rubberball Fatherʼs Ball-Playing Regalia Fatherʼs Ball-Playing Equipo

Truly content were they when they took their Fathersʼ rubberball everyday to their Fathersʼ ballcourt where they went to play; and, for a long time they just played with their Fathersʼ rubberball on their Fathersʼ ball-court.

They swept their Fathersʼ ballcourt making certain that their Fathersʼ ballcourt was kept swept; everyday. But then the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa heard they had returned:

“Who is that who is playing ball over and above our heads; who has begun to play over and above us again; who is that?”

“Just who could that be? Have they no shame to be jumping around up there the way they do?”

“Where is their sense of deference, regard, and respect? They just bounce that ball up and down on those thin plaster walls and thin plaster floors completely ignorant of ancestral tradition and that traditionʼs deep decorum and reverence for the dead; those who are up there have no sense of humility; for truly they play without any consideration nor concern at all for the proper ball-playing behavior and etiquette necessary to play with the rubberball. They are just ill-bred, ill-mannered players who continue to play with their fatherʼs ball without the least sense of propriety; with no sense of proper protocol at all? They are as arrogant and ignorant as they proud and indignant as bigheaded ballplayers can possibly get?”

“Didnʼt Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu die because of their self- aggrandizement before our noble presence?”

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
“Didnʼt they die trying to show off in front of us the way they did without knowing a thing about what they were doing or what they were getting into before they descended here to liven up our lives; the lives of us who are those of Xibʼalbʼa?” “Go then at once to summons them to come here,” roared the Lords. Those who spoke were Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame known as One Death, Seven Death; the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa. One Death and Seven Death sent for their messengers; they called upon them to come to where they were; and so it was that their Messengers came; and when their Messengers came the Lords said this to them: “Say this to them; say this when you arrive with them there up above: ʼCome then-Kepetoq,ʼ say the Lords. ʼHere is where we want you to play, come play with us, in Seven Days we want to play with you here, say the Lords,ʼ this you will say when you arrive with them there,” so then, that was what the Messengers were told to say when the Messengers were sent by the Lords to summons the Boys to come play ball with them in Seven Days. And so the Messengers went with their message along the One Great Wide Road-Jun Nima Jok; it was just one wide open road; it was just one flat open road.

And so it was that they arrived directly at the House of the Boys-chi Kochoch ri Kʼajolabʼ. And so it was that the Messengers-ri Samajel-the Workers of Xibʼalbʼa went straight to their House of the Boys: chi Kochoch ri Kʼajolabʼ.

It was just straightaway that the Messengers of Xibʼalbʼa arrived there with their Grandmother, the Old Woman-Katiʼt.

body:
The Boys were out playing ball on their ballcourt when the Messengers of the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa-AjAwabʼ Xibʼalbʼa arrived with an invitation for them that they left with their Grandmother saying: “The Lords say that they must come here with us. ʼTruly come-Qitzij kepetik-Truly come!ʼ Truly, come play with us say the Lords,” said the Messengers when they left their Lordsʼ message with IxMuqane. Then the Messengers indicated the day they were to arrive; and so it was that the day of the Boys arrival was left well indicated by the Messengers of Xibʼalbʼa: “In Seven Days they, the Boys, are expected to be seen playing ball in Xibʼalbʼa,” this is what they left said to IxMuqane!

Matriarch of the Ixim Winaq Old Women-QaTiʼt-Grandmother
