source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
It wasnʼt ʼhereʼ where they received their power; kiqʼaqʼal and authority to rule; kajawarem; it was ʼthereʼ where they received their sovereign rulership; ʼthereʼ in the Kʼicheʼ; ʼthereʼ in the place from where; from wince they had once come. It was ʼthereʼ where ʼtheyʼ were defeated and subjugated; they, the Big Tribes; Nima Amaqʼ; they, the Small Tribes; Chʼuti Amaqʼ when they were sacrificed before Tojil; when they were made to give their blood; when they were made to be sacrificed for their ʼgathered blood, coagulated bloodʼ when they sacrificed them on their sides; when they sacrificed them through the ribs of their chest as it is said; when they sacrificed them there under their armpits; when they, the People of the Pueblos were sacrificed before their Kabʼawil: Tojil.

This was when those of the Pueblo; Amaqʼ were sacrificed by the Providers-Tzuqul; the Sustainers-Kʼool; when those of the Tribes-Amaqʼ were given up as gifts sacrifice to provide for their Kabʼawil; when the day came when the Pueblos-Amaqʼ were sacrificed as sacred sustenance to sustain their Kabʼawil; the sacred sustenance that was given to provide for and sustain their Kabʼawil: Tojil.

Straight from Tulan came their power; kiqʼaqʼal; directly from Tulan came their power to rule; kajawarem over all the other Tribes; all the different Pueblos; all of the many Amaqʼ so that it was seen that their right to conquer and rule over others came straight from Tulan; Tulan is from where their power came.

And so it was and would always be that their power of rulership; kajawarem; their power of warriorship; kiqʼaqʼal was received there in Tulan, to be taken with them when they left Tulan to return to their Mountain Places of Origin.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
Qʼaqʼal and Tepewal This is when we come to passages when qʼaqʼal and tepewal come to mean power and authority or strength and majesty or rule and authority; all of which will be the power and authority given to Kʼicheʼ Warlords and War Captains who will go off to conquer and subject the Mountain People and Canyon Country to the power and majesty of the Noble Lord of Tollan Tzuy-Wa: Nakxitl Qʼuqʼkumatz known as Sovereign Lord Quetzalcoatl; the Noble Lord Sovereign Plumed Serpent.

Qʼaqʼal and tepewal translated as ʼpowerʼ and ʼrule and authorityʼ are going to be vastly important in the last third of the Popol Wuj. Qʼaqʼal is translated as ʼfireʼ but it is really the ʼburning embers of burning charcoalʼ. So qʼaqʼal that is translated as ʼfireʼ and spoken of as ʼfire and powerʼ were once imagined by the Maya as the burning embers of charcoal-qʼaqʼal that burned as divine fire and sacred embers to consume the sacred sustenance of the human heart burnt on the sacrificial pyre devoured by the Kabʼawil to satisfy their divine appetite and its insatiable hunger for human hearts and human blood to feed those that must be fed.

Remember IxKikʼ and the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa saying: ʼgo ahead and stir up the burning embers of our fires so we can ʼthrow-downʼ the heart of IxKikʼ to smell how it burnsʼ when her heart burnt so sweetly there on the those burning embers that were stirred up in the sacrificial brazier of ritual sacrifice! This is where the power-qʼaqʼal deceive the Lords by blinding the Lords as trickster deities often do to cause disruption in order to transform the what things are done and who gets what when comes to divvying up the sacrificial offering when it comes to the apportionment of sacred sustenance that becomes a reapportionment of sweet smelling gifts of sacrifice.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
Great knowledge came to them in the Dark of Night; in the Darkness genius came to them. Great insight, great understanding came to them in the Dark of Night-chi qʼequmal; in the Darkness they found their genius, their insight. Great wisdom came to them through the sacrificial ordeal they went through there in the Dark Darkness before the Dawn-chi Aqʼabʼal where they watched and waited at the Coming Out Place of the Sun.

This is the divine place and the sacred time when and where the ritual practitioner experiences the relief of the return of the light and warmth of the Sun; the sensation of renewal and rebirth of life in the warmth and in the light after staying focused on the horizon through the ʼedgyʼ Darkness of Night-Aqʼabʼal and ʼthresholdʼ dark before the Dawn-Aqʼabʼal while all the while praying out loud to articulate the needs of their People and their Pueblo to fill the mountain air and ears of their Kabʼawil with their petitionary prayers while all the while making certain to maintain ritual vision and ceremonial focus on the Coming Out Place of the Sun-Relebʼal Qʼij- Place of the Dawn: Saqiribʼal.

So then they came away from there; they just pulled themselves up and left there; leaving behind that place known as the Coming Out Place of the Sun-chi Relebʼal Qʼij; the House of Dawn; the Coming Up Place of the Sun; there in the East: Tulan is its name.

“This here is not our home, letʼs just get going to see where we can go to establish ourselves over there, let us see where we can settle down,” said Tojil.

Truly, it was he-Tojil-who spoke with them, those known and named:

Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ, Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ, Majukʼutaj, Ikʼi Bʼalam “Upon leaving show your gratitude; upon departing leave your thanks; just give of yourself! This then is when you must bleed your ears. This then is when you must sow thorns in your elbows! Perform your sacrifice! This is the way to show your gratitude there before your Kabʼawil!” said Tojil their Kabʼawil. “Utz bʼa la!” they said upon taking leave of the place they came to know: Tulan, Tzuy-Wa. This is the place they pulled themselves up and out of to begin their journey of return back to where they had come.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
Then they bled their ears. They drew blood from their ears when they wept in their song. This is when they came away from Tulan; when they left Tulan weeping as they sang their song of departure; when they sang their song upon abandoning the East at their leaving Tulan.

Truly their hearts cried out when they came away from there; when they pulled themselves up; when they left Tulan; when they abandoned Tulan.

“¡Aqʼaroq! Ayyyayayayay! This is not the place we will watch for the Sunrise. When the Sun is born to shine its light upon the Face of the Earth,” they cried out as they called out to one and all. So then they came away from there; just sleeping alongside the road did they come away from there. And so it was that a few remained where they slept beside the road, a few stayed where they slept; they did not continue on.

Other Tribes rose-up and began moving again, always with their eyes set upon the place of the dawning Sun at the Dawn of the day where the Star shines as a sign at the place where it rise there before the coming forth of the Sun; before the sprouting out of the Sun They just came walking along with their eyes set on the horizon; always with their vision seeking the Star that shines as the sign of the Sun.

This was the remembrance of the ʼDawnʼ in their hearts, in their memory, when they left the Coming Out Place of the Sun; Relebʼal Qʼij when they left the East, when they came away walking from Tulan. Together as ʼOneʼ they passed upon the place there known as Nim Xol-the Great Hollow, the Great Opening as they call it today beside the place known as Karchaj.

And then they arrived atop One Mountain Jun Juyubʼ. There is where all of the Kʼicheʼ People; Kʼecheʼ Winaq gathered together with the other Tribes-Amaqʼ.

This is the place where they celebrated council with one another. This is the place where they gave advice and provided counsel while giving instructions to one another. The name of the mountain today is Chi Pixabʼ: Place of Council; Council Place; Place of Counsel.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
Chi Pixab, Council Place is the name of the mountain where they came together to name one another at Chi Pixabʼ known as Place of Council; Place of Counsel; this is where they took leave of one another.

This is where they acknowledged one another as Kʼecheʼ Amaqʼ which is to say the Kʼicheʼ Pueblo; Kʼicheʼ People; Kʼicheʼ Winaq; Kʼicheʼ Pueblo; Kʼicheʼ Amaqʼ. “In waʼ, in Kʼicheʼ Winaq!

I am here; I am of the Kʼicheʼ People;

I am here who stands before you; I am a member of the Kʼicheʼ People;

I who am here before you stands as a member of the Many Trees People; Kʼicheʼ Winaq: In waʼ, in Kʼicheʼ Winaq!

I who am here; am here as a member of the Kʼicheʼ People.” “And you there, you who are Tamubʼ; Tamubʼ the name of those who are known as the People of the Trunk. Tamubʼ is the name youʼve been named to name the Trunk People, the Pueblo Tamubʼ is who you are,” was what the Tamubʼ were told.

And then it was said, “Ilokʼabʼ, At Ilokʼabʼ, this shall be your name, you the ʼHoney Huntersʼʼ those ʼPeople of Visionʼ as you are spoken of to become the People, the Pueblo you now are: Ilokʼabʼ Winaq!

May that these three branches of the Kʼicheʼ lineages never be lost, for our word is just one-xa junam qatzij-just one and the same shall be our word, our truth, our tradition-xa junam qatzij,” they said when they placed names upon one another.

Then they named the Qʼaqʼchekelebʼ and so the Kaqchikelebʼ is the name they were given. And just like them the Rabʼinalebʼ is the name they were named and who the Rabʼinalebʼ came to be.

These names of the Tribes-Amaqʼ; these names of Pueblos are used today; they are not lost on us today. These are the names the Pueblos; the names of the Pueblos that the People of the Pueblos continue to used to name themselves when they name their names today.

And then there is the Aj Tzʼikina Ja; the Bird House People; Bird House Pueblo and that continues to be their name today: Aj Tzʼikina Ja. These then are the names that they the Pueblos-Amaqʼ; the People-Winaq named one another. This was when they named each other; when they named each otherʼs names as Kʼicheʼ Winaq; Kʼicheʼ Amaqʼ.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
Are kʼu kibʼi, ri xkibʼij chi kibʼil kibʼ. This is how they were named; they named each other by name.

There was the place where they wished to go in order to arrive so they could await the Dawn. It was there in that place that they wanted to get to so that upon their arrival they could watch for the return of the Star that bore up the Sun in his tumpline to carry him up into the Sky.

So they went walking to this place to watch for the Coming Out of the Star- Chʼumil; known as the First One before the Sun-Nabʼe chuwach Qʼij; the First before the Sun; the One coming up before the Birth of the Sun-Qʼij. “There is the place we came from when we divided up to split apart from one another when we abandoned Tulan,” they said to each other; kibʼil kibʼ.

Tormented were their hearts; sorrowful were their souls for the great suffering they experienced for all they had gone through with one another there.

They ate nothing; nothing was eaten by them there; no sustenance was taken by any of them.

They just inhaled the smell of the point of their walking stick; they just breathed in the tips of the walking sticks to take in their scent to give them the feeling they had eaten.

And so it was that they ate nothing while they walked along the way from where they came walking on their long walk from Tulan.

It is not clear as how they crossed the Sea-pa Palo. They crossed the sea as if there were no sea to cross; that is the way they crossed the sea; they just crossed over upon the rocks. For there were just stones; there were just rocks lined-up in a row on the sand where they crossed over the Sea when they crossed over the Sea walking.

And so this then is the naming of this place: Line of Ordered Stones- Cholochik Abʼaj-Ordered Line of Stones and Pulled-Up Sand-Bʼoqotajinaq Sanayebʼ-Raised-Up Sand. These are the names of the places where they crossed- over the Sea. The waters were separated there where they crossed on their way.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
Perhaps this is the remembrance of the places known as los Bajos or the Low-laying areas that form inland seas out in the Petén Jungle. These areas would have to be ʼpassed overʼ by walking pilgrims. Many areas such as these lay between Northern Yucatan where Mayapan and Chichen Itza are found and the distant Kʼicheʼ Highlands; if one were to take a relatively straight line towards the Highlands of Guatemala then one would be forced to pass over these low-lying areas that the Maya must have created their Saq Bʼey or Sacred Road that ran north- south. Is this what the Popol Wuj is talking to us about here in very simple yet revealing ways?

They suffered deep affliction; truly, they felt anguish in their hearts when they took council together as they contemplated what it was that they were obliged to do next. There was nothing for them to eat; but there was something for them to drink as their sustenance; the name of this one drink was ju ukʼ known as jun ukʼi or jukʼi an ancestral drink that came from just one kind of maize-xa juna ixim. Just ʼone kind of maizeʼ was ground fine to create their sacred sustenance that they drank as their one drink of maize: ju ukʼ is its name; jukʼi as it is known.

This line of text is so very, very interesting as it takes us back to the Wooden People and their grinding stones that spoke out to them in significant signifying ways that become significant now as we hear of this primordial maize drink that enables the survival of the First Four Fathers. The First Fathers who are now leading by being led by Tojil their Kabʼawil; the Kabʼawil of the now multiplying-Tamubʼ, Ilokabʼ, Qʼaqʼchikelebʼ, Aj Tzʼikina Ja Pueblos who are growing in number as the Kʼicheʼ People, Kʼicheʼ Pueblo.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
These are those who will always remember their ancestors when they drink their ʼone drink of sustenanceʼ that is remembered when they sow their maize in their milpa and drink this ʼone drink of one variety of maizeʼ in a very subtenant significant sort of way through the spoken phrase: “Ju ukʼ chikiqumej ri xa juna ixim-One drink is what they drank of only one kind of maize.” Remember, remember the grinding stones calling out joli, joli, joli…jukʼi, jukʼi, jukʼi now you know where this comes from: the one primordial maize drink to stave off hunger: jun ukʼ juna ixim or one beverage of one kind of maize; the one maize drink of one kind of maize; one kind of sustenance: jukʼi, jukʼi, jukʼi.

This is when they bore on their back the ʼsacred burdenʼ that they carried to the top of the mountain, the mountain known as Chi Pixabʼ spoken of as Place of Council, Council Place.

They just bore the burden of their divine cargo up the mountainside; those Kabʼawil that they carried were those known and named: Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz.

A Great Fast-Nima Mewajik was carried out by Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ with his woman-rixoqil-his wife Kaqa Paluna-Red Sea Turtle Woman was her name. The same Great Fast-Nima Mewajik was performed by Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ with his wife-rixoqil-his woman Chomi Ja-Shrimp House, Prawn House as she is named.

Majukʼutaj completed his Great Fast-Nima Mewajik with his woman-rixoqil- his wife Tzʼununi Ja-Hummingbird House as she is named, his partner; rikʼulel as she was spoken when she was named as his wife, his partner: rixoqil, rikʼulel. Ikʼi Bʼalam kept a Great Fast-Nima Mewajik like the others; Ikʼi Bʼalam fasted with his woman, his wife, his partner; Kaqix Ja who was known as Scarlet Macaw House.

These ancestral couples carried out their Great Fast-Nima Mewajik there in the dark; there in the darkness that anticipate the coming forth of their Sun; there before the dawning of their Dawn. Great was their affliction; weary with worry were they for their great concern there up on the mountain top known today as Chi Pixabʼ that was their Place of Council known as the Council Place of the Kʼicheʼ People, Kʼicheʼ Pueblo; Kʼicheʼ Winaq, Kʼicheʼ Amaqʼ: Chi Pixabʼ.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
So they spoke again with their Kabʼawil there. This is what was said by: Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz to those known and named: Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ, Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ, Majukʼutaj, Ikʼi Bʼalam.

This then was when their Kabʼawil counseled them on what they were to do with these words of counsel that were words of advice when they celebrated council together on the mountain top of Chi Pixabʼ; the place they that they left when they took leave of this Place of Taking Leave: Chi Pixabʼ. “We should just get going; we must ʼrise-up-yojyakatajikʼ and take leave of this place that is not of our essence; our character; our nature; this place that is not of our way of being; the way of becoming that is our way of being. This place is not our place to be and become who we shall come to be! So let us take leave of it to go somewhere that is of our way of being and becoming!” said the Kabʼawil. “Let us find a place to hide ourselves away. Will not the Dawn soon be upon us? Will not the Dawn of Our Sun soon appear at the Coming Out Place of the Sun: Relebʼal Qʼij?” “Would it not be a disgrace for you-the First Four Fathers-if we-your Kabʼawil-were to be taken as ʼwar captivesʼ by the Warrior People; AjLabʼal? We should be hidden away in a hiding place we ourselves make; or maybe just be kept out of sight behind some kind of hideaway we create: chi tzʼaq!”

“You might then just hide us beside a temple wall-chi tzʼaq. This is where we should be placed for you who are those who perform rituals of sacrifice with Maguey Thorns-Ix AjKʼixbʼ; and, you Ix AjKʼajbʼ who perform penitential acts of sacrificial punishment with your Obsidian Blades. You must make yourselves ready. Each one of us Kabʼawil with their own place; each one with a place of their own,” they said when they spoke; when the Kabʼawil spoke to those who bore them on their backs as their sacred burden.

“Utz bʼa la. Let us just pull ourselves up to get going so we can move out of here to find a place in the forest among the ʼmany trees-kʼechelajʼ for each one us to have our place to hideaway,” said all those who were there to speak to one another while taking council together at Chi Pixabʼ.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
Each one of them carried their deity upon their backs; each group bore their sacred burden of their Kabʼawil.

And so it came to pass that Awilix entered a canyon known as Ewabʼal Siwan; Hideaway Canyon as it is spoken of by all. It was a grand canyon amidst a great forest.

Pa Awilix is the name of this hidden sort of hiding place now; Pa Awilix is the name of this hideaway as this hidden hiding place is known today; the hiding place of Awilix where Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ left his Kabʼawil there in a Hidden Canyon in a Great Forest: Ewabʼal Siwan; Hideaway Canyon; Hideaway Ravine; the Hidden Hideaway in the Hidden Canyon; Ewabʼal Siwan as it is known. Each of the Kabʼawil from Tulan Tzuy Wa was left in their own hiding place in an orderly fashion: these Kabʼawil of the First Fathers were hidden one after another: Awilix was first.

Next came Jaqawitz who was brought to a mountain-top where there stood a mountain-top temple; this mountain-top temple was One Great Red House-Jun Nima Kaqa Ja.

This is where he, Jaqawitz, was left; when Jaqawitz was left upon this one great temple house that stood upon this one mountain-top known for its one great red house. This is the mountain-top known as Kaqajawitz: Red House Mountain. Jaqawitz was the second deity that was hidden by them; but they did not hide him in a forest because they hid Jaqawitz on top of a Great Red Temple House-chuwi Jun Nima Kaqaja.

Jaqawitz is the name of the mountain today; the mountain upon which was founded the town known as Jaqawitz. Majukʼutaj was left here along with his Kabʼawil that he carried known as Jaqawitz. This is the name of the deity that will become the name of the mountain citadel known and named Jaqawitz.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
Jaqawitz was the second deity that was hidden by them; they did not hide him in a forest but up on top of a ʼcleared-off; cleaned-offʼ mountain known as saqi juyubʼ or cleared-off mountain. This ʼcleared-off; cleaned-offʼ mountain top is where they placed Jaqawitz which was an open mountain that was cleared of all the trees and vines; it was just a cleaned off mountain top known and named Saqawitz for it was a ʼcleared-off mountainʼ which made it a ʼOpen Mountain or Jaqawitzʼ because it was a mountain-top that was completely ʼcleaned-offʼ to be completely ʼopened-upʼ upon on top so they called it Jaqawitz: open mountain since ʼjaqʼ is to ʼopenʼ up. Today it is known as ʼChuwi Juyubʼ or ʼMountain Topʼ that is remembered by all as a Sacred Mountain; Saqawitz.

And so it was that Jaqawitz the Kabʼawil of Majukʼutaj was left on top of a cleared-off kind of cleaned-off sort of mountain-top where there was a Great Temple known as the Red House that was a Sacred Temple House placed up on this wide-open mountain-top where Majukʼutaj stayed alongside his Kabʼawil Jaqawitz on a sacred mountain-top that was an open mountain-top that was a cleaned-off kind of cleared-off mountain-top that in time would be known as: Kaqawitz, Jaqawitz, Saqawitz because of how Jaqawitz was left there with Majukʼutaj.

Jaqawitz; Kaqajawitz; Saqawitz; Qʼaqʼawitz; Jaqʼawitz; Witz-Mountain; Open Mountain Top or Chuwi Juyubʼ or the Above the Mountain; Up-Upon the Cleared-off Red Temple Mountain Jaqawitz becomes the mountain citadel known as Jaqawitz where Majukʼutaj leaves his Kabʼawil Jaqawitz that is also known as Kaqajawitz and Saqawitz and Jaqawitz in master play Nawal Transformation combined with the ʼinvisibilityʼ of Majukʼutaj: Nobody Is Here who seems to be coming in and out of sight.

None of which one could possibly understand from a ʼliteralʼ translation and interpretation of Popol Wuj! So there you have it; right here, a clear, clean kind of open understanding of Jaqawitz where soon there will be great conflict that will lead to a ʼmagical battleʼ in which Great Pots of Bees and Wasps that are Sacred Pots of Bees and Wasps will be ʼopened-jaqaʼ by being broken open-jaqʼaʼ which is to say smashed open-jaqʼaʼ to release these vicious vindictive flying insects with a deadly sting who are the embodiment of the ʼanimal companionʼ or ʼnagualʼ or ʼanimal transformsʼ of the Warlord Majukʼutaj who along with his Kabʼawil Jaqawitz will become the Noble Lord and Ruler of Jaqawitz the mountain top citadel of Jaqawitz.

Majukʼutaj is the Third-Rox of the First Four Fathers who receives Jaqawitz as his Kabʼawil at Tulan to then leave Tulan by abandoning Tulan when leaving Tulan Tzuy-Wa.

body:
I suspect there is some sort of auspicious kind of propitious type of confusion created here in the ʼhidingʼ of the Kabʼawil in the hidden mountain places by leaving one of the Kabʼawil in the open in plain sight. This is Jaqawitz who is left on the ʼOpen Mountain- Saqawitzʼ as the Kabʼawil of Majukʼutaj-Black Panther of the Western Cardinal Direction of the Black Night; the Falling Down Place of the Sun in the West who is the Invisible One- Majukʼutaj.

It is he who leaves us with a great many mythic names and images to fire-up our imagination that is fully engaged in the mythic metaphors formed by the mythic figures and mythic archetypes that bring to life an imaginal realm as alive with mythic images as one could ever wish or want for. Yes indeed, our mythic imagination is now burning bright as we open up to a most fascinating imaginal world atop this cleared-off Mountain Top where the Kʼicheʼ Winaq will establish themselves for the first time a People who are a Pueblo of Warlords who do not conquer the Mountain People. No, the Kʼicheʼ Lords known as los Tojiles will only defend their Women and Children; Daughters and Sons; Vassals and Subject atop the Primordial Mountain known and named as Jaqawitz and this story of their defending their Mountain Place is what shall be told here. But there is more because there will soon be built a ʼgreat walled palisadeʼ atop Jaqawitz the Mountain that will form and shape the Citadel of Jaqawitz of the Kabʼawil Jaqawitz on the Mountain Jaqawitz so that Jaqawitz the Kabʼawil who was ʼjustʼ left with Majukʼutaj on the Mountain of Jaqawitz will become the Lord and Ruler of the mountain-top citadel of Jaqawitz. Jaqawitz the Mountain Citadel that is established on the Open-Mountain; Jaqa-Witz that is the place once known as Kaqajawitz because of the Great Red House Temple of Sacrifice that made this a Saqawitz; Sacred Mountain that is a Dawning Mountain-top; Saqiribʼal that opens to a clear view of the Relebʼal Qʼij to watch and wait for the Great Star; Nima Chumil that is the very same place where the Great Red Temple House; Nima Kaqaja was built upon the Open Cleared- Off Mountain of Saqawitz.

body:
I hope this detailed explanation is of some benefit to your enriched understanding of this most esoteric section of Popol Wuj. One must come to appreciate the ability of the Maya Scribe to create a kind of nawal sort of confusion as a person becomes a place to become a divinity to become a citadel to become a mountain top that is named one name than another all in order to hide the Kabʼawil Jaqawitz in a net of confusion in order to create the sense of everything coming out of nothing to return to nothing.

For some reason the Kabʼawil say there are very good reasons to think and believe they might be captured. So it would be best that they are hidden from those who ʼmightʼ be ʼtrackingʼ them. And so it is the Kabʼawil Jaqawitz is best hidden in a Great Red House and being it a Red House it is a Temple of Sacrifice giving the name of the Mountain Top: Kaqa Ja Witz or Kaqajawitz. All of which will ʼthrow offʼ those ʼinvisible enemy forcesʼ in search of the First Four Fathers and their Kabʼawil who have returned to the Mountains of the Kʼicheʼ as Noble Lords of Tolan Tzuy-Wa who want to settle themselves among the ʼMountain Peopleʼ mentioned earlier in our mythic narrative.

Now we are in those Mountains with Majukʼutaj which is best translated as the ʼInvisible Oneʼ which is one of the names of Tezcatlipoca which the name of Heart of the Sky; Ukʼuʼx Kaj that is the name of Jun Raqan Kaqulja; the One Footed One; the Smoking Mirror: Tezcatlipoca. You get the idea; I hope you get the idea because it isnʼt at all obvious.

But once you ʼgetʼ a ʼsenseʼ of ʼitʼ ʼoneʼ canʼt help but ʼfeelʼ the ʼgeniusʼ of this ʼnawalʼ of ʼinvisibilityʼ and ʼbeingʼ going ʼpoofʼ into ʼthin airʼ which is quite wonderful but more than likely best pulled off through the ʼperformanceʼ of ʼstorytellingʼ by Kʼicheʼ Maya Mother- Fathers of the Ancient Word: Chuch-Qajaw Ojer Tzij.

body:
These Masters of the Ancient Word played with this ʼnaming of the namesʼ that forms as it shapes the ʼInvisible Senseʼ that comes forth from the name of Majukʼutaj. Majukʼutaj the One; Jun who is Ma-Jun; No One that becomes Maju; Not One to create the invisible name ʼNo One is Hereʼ Ma-Jun-Kʼo-Taj that become Majukʼutaj.

Nothing is here to find or to track so that there is ʼNothing to Showʼ or ʼNo Sign to be Seenʼ or the ʼInvisible One; Titlacauanʼ all of which makes one think of Tezcatlipoca as Titlacauan; Invisible One and his wily ways as the beguiling Lord of Mysterious Comings and Goings and Ruler of Nawal Trickster Deities such as these Four Jaguar Lords of the Kʼicheʼ.

Tezcatlipoca is the ʼObsidian Mirror that smokesʼ in a mirror of divination into which everything can be seen by this Changing and Transforming Trickster Deity Extraordinaire: Tezcatlipoca.

Tezcatlipoca is also known as ʼHe who makes Himself; Moyocoyaniʼ who is he who gives great wealth in the form of ornamentation and embellishment and it is he who takes them away. Remember this, oh please do remember this: the one who gives prosperity to then take it away from those who do not respect him and his way!

So do not get confused while watching how the ʼbreaking open or jaqaʼ of the ʼSacred Pots; Kukʼubʼ once translated as ʼGod Potsʼ that are the ʼTamale Potsʼ that are ʼbroken openʼ inside the entrance of Jaqawitz; the Citadel. This ʼbreaking open; jaqaʼ is really a ʼsmashing open or jaqʼaʼ which is just a change in the inflection of the guttural sounding q to occlusive sounding guttural qʼ that for the Maya is heard loud and clear!

body:
This smashing open of the Sacred Pots or the jaqʼa Kukʼubʼ is when and where and what causes the deadly stinging Metallic Black Wasps-Sitaʼl and blistering bite of Big Bad Bees- Wonon come out of nowhere like the unseen, unnamed Tezcatlipoca who is known as the Invisible Enemy and/or the Enemy on Both Sides to win the conflict that is the battle that is the war of Jaqawitz or Jaqʼawitz when the Sacred Pots of Sustenance where tamales are cooked up are ʼopened upʼ by having the tops being ʼsmashed open or broken open to name the name of his sacred mountain as Jaqʼawitz not just Jaqawitz.

This is when the United Forces of the Kʼicheʼ will be attacked by the United Forces of the Pueblos; ri Amaqʼ; the Tribes of the Mountain Places and Canyon Country who will be defeated by Tojil. Tojil as the protecting and guiding Kabʼawil of the Kʼicheʼ who will provide counsel in the form of strategic advice to the Lords of Kʼicheʼ on how to gather together the Sitaʼl and Wonon; Black Stinging Wasps and Big Round Bees to destroy and devastated the Pueblos and Tribes of the Mountains and Canyons.

This shamanic transformation of the Kabʼawil Jaqawitz into becoming his Nagual Animal Transform of Wasps and Bees is one Mesoamericaʼs greatest archetypal examples of Nawal Winaq controlling the natural world and the Ancestral Beings that exist within it to be called upon as the ʼmagical alliesʼ of the Kʼicheʼ People of the Pueblo Kʼicheʼ.

This is not the only time these bees and those wasps will be brought to life by Tojil to take revenge on the arrogant, self-aggrandizing enemies of the Kʼicheʼ Winaq and their Kʼicheʼ

Kabʼawil: Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz and Nikʼaj Taqʼaj.

Enough is enough with all of this interpretive narrative as valuable as it is; it isnʼt the original Ojer Tzij; Ancient Word of this Book of Council; Popol Wuj.

body:
In just one place were those named: Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ, Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ, Majukʼutaj, Ikʼi Bʼalam. It was they who came together as one in the forest as AjKʼixbʼ, AjKajbʼ; for they were one now with one-an-other as when they left; yet they did not return as they had gone away in search of ʼsomeoneʼ who could guide and protect them along the way.

These are those who journeyed to Tollan Tzuy-Wa for a reason; so when they returned they were not the same as when they left. They left as Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ, Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ, Majukʼutaj, Ikʼi Bʼalam to return as the AjKʼixbʼ, AjKajbʼ from Tollan.

As ʼOneʼ they watched and waited for the Dawn up above on the mountain Jaqawitz, as it is named; Jaqawitz then was the name of the Mountain-top upon which they watched and waited for the Dawn: Saqirik.

Those who were there were the AjKʼixbʼ, AjKajbʼ known as the First Four Fathers: Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ, Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ, Majukʼutaj, Ikʼi Bʼalam. ʼXa Junʼ; As ʼJust One-Xa Junʼ they awaited the Dawn there above atop the Mountain Jaqawitz is its name: Jakʼawitz ubʼi. At a short distance between where they were gathered together at Jaqawitz were hidden the Kabʼawil of the Tamubʼ and Ilokabʼ. The Tamubʼ hid their Kabʼawil at the place named Amaqʼ Tam; Pueblo of the Tree Trunk; Tribe of the Tree Trunk: Amaqʼ Tam. This is where the Kabʼawil of the Tamubʼ was placed; and, there is where the Kabʼawil of the Tamubʼ or ʼTree Trunk Peopleʼ celebrated the Dawn; chiriʼ xsaqir wi-there they celebrated the Dawning of the Dawn together as a People; as One; together as Pueblo; those whose name is named: Tamubʼ.

The Ilokabʼ who were the ʼHoney Huntersʼ hid their Kabʼawil in the place known as Amaqʼ Ukʼin Kʼat-ʼthe Burn of the Sunʼ or ʼWhere the Sun Burntʼ or ʼthe Maize Drinkʼs Fireʼ ʼFire to Cook the Maize Drinkʼ or ʼWarp of the Weave of the Harvest Netʼ or ʼHarvest Net of the Jocoteʼ Ukʼin Kʼat is the name of the hiding place of their Kabʼawil. It was they who watched for the Dawn, Saqirik a short distance between one another.

body:
The Sun dawned upon them here in a place named after their name known as the Pueblo of the Trunk: Amaqʼ Tam. Amaqʼ Tam is their name, the name given to their home, the home of the Tamubʼ. Amaqʼ Uqʼin Kʼat is the place where the Ilokabʼ watched for the Dawn, and this is where the Kabʼawil of the Ilokʼabʼ was placed there just a short distance between; betwixt the mountains-xa kok uxol juyubʼ of the other Tribes known as the Pueblos; Amaqʼ who were ʼJust One-Xa Junʼ with those of Tojil.

It was there that the Rabʼinalebʼ, Qʼaqʼchekelebʼ, Aj Tzʼikina Ja gathered together with the Small Tribes-Chʼuti Amaqʼ and Big Tribes-Nima Amaqʼ. In just One Place they came to a halt; they stopped there together; the detained themselves there as Just One People and, as Xa Jun-Just One together they gathered together to celebrate council as Just One Pueblo-Xa Jun Amaqʼ to watch, to wait for the Dawn.

In just one place they waited for the coming out of the Great Star-relik uloq Nima Chʼumil-Morning Star, the Great Star that they called Ikʼoqʼij by name.

This is the Great Star known as: “First to come out before the Face of the Sun-Nabʼe chel uloq chuwach Qʼij. ¡TA SAQIROQ! When Dawn Came! When the Dawn of the Sun Came!”

“Here comes the bright-shining Star; the Sun-Bearer-Ikʼoqʼij that rises just before the Dawn,” they said. They were ʼJust One-Xa Junʼ there: Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ, Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ, Majukʼutaj, Ikʼi Bʼalam. They could not sleep, nor did they rest for the worry of their weary souls; for their restless hearts were filled with woe; they just felt an anguished agony there before its imminent arrival; distressed, distraught were their anxious souls as they watched waiting before the Dawn; as they watched waiting there before the Rising Sun. And that is how it was when one of them said: “It is not so sweet this place that we have come to here. ¡Aqʼaroq! ¡Aqʼaroq!”

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
“If only we could see the birth of the Sun! What have we done, we were once the same as one another on our mountain place-qajuyubʼal-from where we come; from where we came.” “We just abandoned it; we just divided up and separated when before we lived as if we were one,” they said when they spoke together with one another.

This is when they spoke to one-an-other as they pondered their pitiable plight; as they faced the fear, as the faced their fright; as they cried out into the deep dark of night there before the Dawn.

This is when they spoke; for their hearts were now desperate to see the Dawn: Saqirik.

Their hearts could not be consoled, for they grieved to see the Dawn with the Rising of the Sun. Maja kʼut chi kubʼaroq kikʼux chi re usaqirik. The ones that were tranquil, the ones who felt contentment were the Kabʼawil in the Canyons-pa taq Siwan, in the Forests-pa taq Kʼechelaj among the flowering bromeliad, among the hanging moss; there amongst the Many Trees of the Great Forest is where there Kabʼawil were in a contented state of great tranquility.

It was not upon wooden pedestals that they were placed; it was in the forest that they felt at home.

So then they were the first to speak, those named: Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz.

Great was their destiny; they were strong of heart; ancestral anima animated their ancient souls; this is why they were greater than all other Kabʼawil of all the other Tribes; of all the other Pueblos; of all the other People; truly, great was the destiny of the Kabʼawil: Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz.

And so truly great was their destiny before all the other Kabʼawil of all the other Pueblos. Great were their ancient ancestral powers of transformation that was their nawal essence; that was their nawal condition; that was their nawal character and nature; the nawal nature of these Kabʼawil that were Nawal Ancestors in every way, shape, and form; whose magical changing and transforming nawal ways made these Kabʼawil who they were and how they were known and named: Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
They were those who moved about in the world on two legs and on four legs to open the way; to lead the way; to guide the way to become who they need be at the moment in order to move about as they wished and willed themselves to appear among the People of the Pueblos; at first to cause amazing wonder and astonishing awe; but then to create shocking fright and surprising fear.

For truly their presence caused fearful fright in all the Pueblos and all their People whose hearts; whose souls could only be calmed by: Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ, Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ, Majukʼutaj, Ikʼi Bʼalam.

Yet their hearts found no bitterness towards the Kabʼawil they had carried for so long on their backs ever since their departure when they walked away from Tulan Tzuy Wa; the place known as Relebʼal Qʼij: the Coming Out Place of the Sun. It was just there in the Forest; pa Kʼechelaj when the Dawn; Saqiribʼal came for Tojil, pa Tojil; for Awilix, pa Awilix; for Jaqawitz, pa Jaqawitz as it is said today.

Xawi kʼu chiriʼ xkʼoje wi pa Kʼechelaj are Saqiribʼal pa Tojil; pa Awilix; pa Jaqawitz; kuchaʼxik wakamik.

It was there in the forest atop their Place of Dawn-Saqiribʼal-Dawning Mountain when the Dawn came for Tojil; for Awilix; for Jaqawitz as it is said today.

This then was the Sowing; this then was the Dawning of Our Grandfathers; QaMam, Our Fathers-Qajaw at this Place of Sowing, Place of Dawning; Ewaxibʼal; Saqiribʼal. For there it was there in the Forest; Kʼicheʼlaj of Saqiribʼal; of the Mountain of Dawn that Sunrise came when Dawn arrived for Tojil, for Awilix, for Jaqawitz as they are spoken of today. This was the Sowing-Ewaxibʼal; this was the Dawning; Saqiribʼal of Our Grandfathers, Our Fathers: QaMam, QaQajaw.

Xa kʼu Jun Xechawax wi; Xsaqir wi ronojel Amaqʼ.

There was just One Sowing; just One Dawning for all of the Pueblos. Waʼe chiqabʼij chik Saqirik; uwachinik Qʼij, Ikʼ, Chʼumil. Here we shall tell next of the Dawning; the Appearance of the Sun, Moon, Star.

Here now we shall tell next of the Dawning; when we tell of the appearance of the Sun, Moon, and Star. Here then is the telling of the Dawning; the telling of the Emergence of the Face of the Sun; of the Moon; of the Star.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
Great was the contentment of Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ, Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ, Majukʼutaj, Ikʼi Bʼalam when they saw the Morning Star-Ikʼoqʼij-when it came out first, sparkling in the Sky it sprouted forth as it came up and out First-Nabʼe before the Sun.

This then was when they unbound to unbundle their Incense-Pom-Copal that came all the way from the Relebʼal Qʼij; these were bundles of Copal-Pom-Incense that they carried back from the Coming Out Place of the Sun.

Their hearts delighted in their untying to unravel the three different bundles of incense given as gifts of gratitude; given as gifts of thanks; given as gifts that came from the thankfulness of their hearts and souls:

Mixtam Pom; Mictlan Pom was the incense that Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ brought.

Kawistan Pom was the incense Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ carried with him.

Kabʼawil Pom was the incense that Majukʼutaj bore on his back.

These three Noble Lords of these three Noble Lineages brought back three varieties of Pom: Mixtam Pom; Kawistan Pom; Kabʼawil Pom.

This is what they burned their Pom in the direction of the Sunrise, when the Sky brightened; when it whitened; when it lightened with nostalgic reminiscence; xesaqbʼisanik; with the heartfelt remembrance of the Oriente at the Coming Out Place of the Sun-Relebʼal Qʼij. So this then was when they wept with happiness; sweetly they wept with contentment when the Sky began to brighten the Face of the Earth.

This was when they thought upon the Dawn at the Coming Out Place of the Sun; when they contemplated from where they had come there before the arrival of their first Dawning of their Sun.

This then was when they burnt their beloved incense; their sacred incense; their blessed incense; their precious incense: Loqʼolaj Pom. They burnt it there in the direction of the Rising Sun.

So this then was when they wept again; this time they wept because they did not see it; for they did not see the Birth of the Sun-Ralaxik Qʼij. They did not see it yet despite the Sky whitening as began brightening to then begin lightening up the horizon without the Sun ever being born.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
And then it came; the Sun came up; when at first it began show it came up nice and slow; and then up it rose as it rose up and up; and as it rose up and up it grew and grew; this then was when it began to grow and grow when the Sun came up to show its face at the Coming Out Place of the Sun, Relebʼal Qʼij; when the Sun finally rose it climbed up into the Sky up and above the House of the Dawn; there at the Coming Out Place of the Sun...chilaʼ pa Relebʼal Qʼij.

They were all made content; content with the rising Sun were they all; all those who were there; the Small Animals; the Big Animals; Chʼuti Chikop; Nimaʼ Chikop; they were just so very content with the emergence of the Sun; with the sunrise there at dawn the Animals were all made content.

All of them came out to the waterʼs edge; there beside the streams; there beside the rivers; they came out and on to the rims of the canyons and ravines.

They were there on the points of mountain; they came right out upon the outcrops of the rocks there on the mountains; they were there in the mountains out on the points, promontories, and peaks.

Just as one they gazed upon the direction of the rising Sun; there in the direction of the Dawn, in the direction of the Coming Out Place of the Sun: Relebʼal Qʼij they just held their gaze watching with great delight as the rising Sun rose in the Sky. So then Koj-Puma and Bʼalam-Jaguar roared with the first cries of the Guarda Barranco Chajal Siwan; this Brown-backed Solitaire the primordial birdsong of the dawn she sang like a flute, Kʼeletzu is her name, she sang like a flute of the canyon; like a flute did she sing as she sang her song into the canyon with its chasm of silence there at dawning place of the Sun; at the sunrise place of the Dawn.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
Guarda Barranco-Cotora Parlanchin-Chajal Siwan-Guardian of the Canyon is this beloved birdʼs name; this Brown-backed Solitaire sung her long sonorous song; she sang like a flute; she sang her song a dawn; she woke-up singing and kept singing all morning long as she sang her song echoing up and down the canyon walls; just singing as she moved along as she sang her song that she began singing when she rose at dawn to sing her song that rose up and dropped down with its jingle-jangle sort of metallic flute sound; she sung out at the first sight of the dayʼs bright warm light that arrived with the first rays of dawn of all the days that rose up just for her so she could sing her song there at dawn in the first light of the sun and its ancient way of waking the day with birdsong at dawn and again at dusk when Chajal Siwan sang her song in the rising and falling Sun; in the first and last light of the Day this is when she sung: saqnatanoj.

Truly, all the animals were filled with contentment; so, so sweet were their hearts made by the light; by the warmth of the Sun. They opened their wings wide: Eagle, Kot; White Zopilote, Kuch; Small Birds, Chʼuti Tzʼikin; Big Birds, Nima Tzʼikin they stretched their wings out wide to welcome home the Sun.

There on their knees kneeling-xukuxinaq before the presence of the Sun were they, those of the Maguey Spine-AjKʼixbʼ those of the Obsidian Blade- AjKajbʼ. They were there on their knees kneeling-xukulem; mejlem-kneeling on their knees giving thanks with great respect; giving praise with high regard they knelt to give thanks and praise for the Dawning Sun at the Break of Day; as it is said; as they say.

The AjKʼixbʼ knelt there; those who performed blood sacrifice with spines knelt before the Dawn; those who performed sacrifice with their Stingray Spines knelt their before the Sun; those there with their Maguey Thorns were made content with the emergence of the Sun; with the arrival of the Dawn.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
The AjKʼajbʼ knelt with their Obsidian Blades; those who practiced sacrifice with Obsidian Blades knelt on their knees showing their gratitude for truly content were they with the arrival and appearance; entrance and emergence of the Dawning Light of the Rising Sun.

Great was their contentment; great was their satisfaction those who were filled with gratitude; those who were filled with thanks; those who were they of the Maguey Thorn; those who were they of the Stingray Spine: AjKʼixb.

Great was their contentment; great was their satisfaction those who were filled with gratitude; those who were filled with thanks; those who were they of the Obsidian Blade: AjKajb. Those who performed punishing penitential acts of self-sacrifice; those that practiced the blood-letting; blood-gathering ways of self-sacrifice each in their own ancient ancestral way; each with their sacred sacrificial way were there together as Just One-Xa Jun face to face with radiant, resplendent Face of the Sun.

These AjKʼixbʼ, AjKajbʼ were of the Tamubʼ, Ilokʼabʼ who were as happy and content as those of Rabinal, Qʼaqʼchikelebʼ, Aj Tzʼikina Ja; who were happy and content as those of Tujal Ja, Uchabʼa Ja, and those of Kibʼa Ja, AjBatena Ja; and, Yaki Tepew.

How many People; how many Pueblos who were there now that stood before the Dawn! Innumerable people were there now standing before the Sun but there was only One Dawn for all the many Tribes; Amaqʼ when the Sun rose that Day at Dawn.

For the Dawn had dawned at the Coming Out Place of the Sun: pa Relebʼal Qʼij; it had come; the Sun rose up as all watched and waiting while pleading and praying that it would and now the could say: Our Dawn has come for Our Sun.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
And so it was that the Face of the Earth dried up immediately because of the Sun, just like a person was the Sun when he showed his burning face; when his scorching face appeared it instantly dried the Face of the Earth-Uwach Ulew; the Face of the Earth was toasted dry; it was baked dry as soon as he-the Sun-showed his hot burning, blistering Face; the searing face of the sweltering hot Sun dried the Face the Face of the Earth leaving it completely dried out; burnt to the bone. Before the searing, scorching Face of the Sun came-out the Face of the Earth had always been a wet, watery place; before the emergence of the Sun the Earth had been a mushy kind of marshy place. This is how the Earth was before the Sun came out; before the Sun came up the Face of the Earth was as very soggy, swampy place.

But then the Sun rose just like a human being, like a person did the Sun rise; and when it rose the Sun was so hot and dry that no one could endure its red hot heat, one could not survive the sizzling heat of the Sun. But he only showed his face when he was born; so that later on all that remained of him was his mirrored reflection; the Sun mirrored his reflection once he passed the mid-point of the Day when the Sun stood straight-up over the Face of the Earth.

“Itʼs not the same Sun that appears to us today,” says their Ancient Word.

And so, just like that, in an instant, they were turned to stone: Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz with all the other Kabʼawilal, with all the other Divinities that took the form of Puma, Koj; Jaguar, Bʼalam; Rattlesnake, Sochoj; and Fer-de-Lance- Qʼanti-Barba Amarilla spoken of originally: Koj, Bʼalam, Sochoj, Qʼanti the most dangerous devourers of human flesh in all the land; those whose poisonous venomous bite was more than enough to kill one dead.

This was when Saqi Kʼoxol, the Lord of the Mountain-el Dueño de la Montaña-hid himself up in the branches of the trees when the three of them appeared there; there at emergence of the Sun, Moon, Star; Qʼij, Ikʼ, Chʼumil.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
This then was when the Sun, Moon, and Star appeared before all of them there who were the dangerous, deadly ones who when struck by the burning, blistering rays of the Sun were turned to stone; the Deadly Animals were turned to stone for they were transformed by the Sun and turned to Stone. The wild animals and guardians of the trees; the vipers there in the vines were petrified, they were left hard as rocks; they were turned to stone by the hot, dry Face of the Sun.

Had these wild voracious animals not been turned to stone we might not be here today: Koj-Puma, Bʼalam-Jaguar, Sochoj-Rattlesnake, Qʼanti-Qʼantil are all ravenous animals who were innumerable before the Dawn; before emergence of the Sun; before the Coming out of the Dawning Sun. Without Saqi Kʼoxol perhaps we would not be alive today; had the First Animals-Nabʼey Chikop-Original Animals not been turned to stone by the petrifying heat of the Sun, we might not be here at all.

Their hearts filled with great joy and happiness; their souls filled with great contentment and ease the moment the Sun sprouted out of the Earth; when Dawn illuminated the Face of the Earth with its bright shining light; the Dawning Sun just shimmered as it shined for all those who were there at the Coming Out Place of the Sun: Relebʼal Qʼij. Great was their delight; great was their satisfaction, those known as:

Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ, Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ, Majukʼutaj, Ikʼi Bʼalam; they were made content; finally at ease for their hearts were made sweet; with the peace they felt with the Dawn of their Sun-Xsaqirik.

body:
Mythic Time; Mythic Belonging; Mythic Divinity Being At Home in the World of the Divine Ancestors Being at Home in the Imaginal Realm of Myth This is the mythic power of ʼentering the word to enter into the mythic momentʼ by stepping out of the terror of history to step into the transcendence of the mythic present. There is a sense of belonging to a place and a people that provides human beings with a sense of being at home in the world. This sense of being at home in the world is to feel that one belongs in this world comes through myths of that come from the place and people that form and shape the myth of being and belonging in the world; the myth that forms and shapes the place and peopleʼs sense of being and belong in the World.

This is the ʼcontentmentʼ that the Popol Wuj speaks of when it says, “they were happy, they were contentʼ yes they were because they felt at home in the world in which the Sun Rises and the Dawn comes so the seed sprouts and cane grows so that the People of the Maize are at one with Maize that is One with the Sun with its nourishing light and its nurturing warm. When human beings live in a myth that lives within them and that myth tells of the ways of the people and the ways of the place then you can be sure a Human Being feels at Home in the World that is the World they also feel they belong to through the myth of being and becoming that gives a person a sense of belonging.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
Perhaps best of all myth teaches us compassion for other as it opens up to a deep knowledge of the People and Places from where and who the myths we read and engage with comes from. In this sense myth is perhaps the most valuable source and resource for understanding the way the People see and understand the World that the myth comes from. What could be more valuable than this in ones study of myth? This must be how the Popol Wuj was once lived by the Kʼicheʼ Maya and all these other Tribes mentioned here that are the Maya People; Maya Pueblos who lived through this Ancient Ancestral Account of the Sowing and the Dawning. This feeling of being at Home in the Word in order to belong in the World is brought forth in a very subtle way through this Ancient Account that brings forth a sense of temporal transcendence.

This entering into transcendent time is made possible by the performer of the Ancestral Account and the audience of the Ancestral Account enters mythic time through the continue refrain watching and waiting for the Dawn. This Dawn of the Sun that is anticipated through the text repeating over and over that the Dawn was getting closer and closer for the time was coming nearer and nearer to when the Sun, Moon, and Star were about to cross over head of Tzʼaqol, Bʼitol.

And then it happens the Dawn comes and suddenly we enter the warmth and light of the first rays of the Sun as our nostalgic remembrance takes us back to the very first page of Popol Wuj where the Maya Scribe say this is the description, revelation, and manifestation of the expression of the Ancient Word; Ancestral Account of the Sowing and the Dawning of Life and the Peopling and Populating of the Face of the Earth. Here we are with the Pueblos being named at the Sowing and the Dawning.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
IxMuqane brought for the Sowing-Ewaxibʼal by naming the names of the Place where the Maize Harvest are sown in the Middle of the House; Middle of the Harvest and now the Sun has Dawn and its heat has dried out a very mushy marshy Face of the Earth. We are at Home in the World for we have formed and shaped it through the Former, the Shaper-Tzʼaqol, Bʼitol. We have become Tzʼaqol, Bʼitol through the mysterious magic that is a miracle of our mythic imagination with its capacity to mold and model the Imaginal Realm of the Maya Myth of the Sun and Maize.

We have entered the imaginal realm of a very real natural world of the Kʼicheʼ Maya with their Mountains and Plains and their Mountain Place and Canyon Country. Here we are at Home in a World in which we very much belong because we know the story that tells of the Sky- Earth; Lake-Sea that is the Natural World that Formed as it Shaped the forming and shaping of this Ancient Ancestral Narrative of the People of Maize: Ixim Winaq. This you know only too well ʼas ifʼ it were the most important aspect of this Interpretation of this Translation of Popol Wuj. We are made to feel ʼas ifʼ we were the Former, the Shaper through the transformative power of the mythic imagination through its capacity and capability to release us from the present moment by entering the mythic moment when the Sun, Moon, and Star are about to pass overhead in the Imaginal Realm to announce the arrival of the Dawn in our mythic imagination that is fed by our life experience in the real world of the Face of the Earth and its relationship with the Sun, Moon, and Stars both Day and Night; Dawn and Dusk as well as Mid-Day and Mid-Night. We have entered all these times in our Mythic Imagination imagining this very real imaginal world of myth that reflect reality in this reality that reflects myth. Enter Trickster with his Obsidian Mirror with plenty of smoke and even more mist.

This brings up the perennial idea that ʼmyths are things that never were but always areʼ which is to say myths exist in the present through our mythic imagination and its ability to bring to life the imaginal realm of myth so that we might transcend reality by transcending ordinary time and space by entering the word of myth to enter the way of myth leading to the world of myth: the Imaginal Realm of the Divine Ancestors.

This is how we create an ecstatic experience that takes transports our soul by entering myth through the ʼeyeʼ of the mythic imagination in order to exist in mythic time and mythic space. This is where we find a deep sense of belonging as the landscape we live in is reflected in the sacred landscape we imagine in myth; just as the people we live with such as the Maya we live with here in the Highlands mirror the Nawal Ancestors and Mythic Figures that live in our mythic imagination to feel a deep sense of belonging in this world that we feel very much at home.

This is the beauty of myth; it tells the deepest truths of human relationships and those human relationships connection and communication with the real world in which we live. Myths speak to us of the most important aspects of life and we can be sure the truths we find in myth have been contemplated by human beings and their divinities for tens of thousands of years. Yet we doubt all of this because of the arrogant and pride of the self-aggrandizing mind of the rational, lineal, analytical, sorts of materialist minds that think they are the end all to all of human conscious which is what it is and what is a joke if it were not so very psychologically infirm. But we give myth the benefit of the doubt in order to really enter into its original genius then we come to realize the highly level of civilizing content that exists within myth.

This is where myth is played out through the movement of the Constellations of the Night Sky that tell us of the mythic events; mythic figures; mythic places that are brought to life through the mythic narratives told by Ancient Ones who shine as bring lights in the dark of the Night. This is why the Dawn is so bright because that is when the Ancestors speak to us through the movements of Nature and the ancestral language of the dawn song and its being sung to speak and communicate with us through the language of the birds; language of the breeze; language of light; language of the sunlight as it plays with the sparkling spectrum of light that twinkle as iridescent colors on the dewdrops at the tip of the leaves in the Sun at Sunrise with its magic white light of the calm and collected; settled and silent; still and quiet sky at Dawn.

This is the language of myth spoken in the landscape to connect with the descendants and their infinite ways of communicating with those who want to connect with the Ancient Ones who transform into whatever they must to connect with their replacements on the Face of the Earth; the Nawal Ancestors in all the forms and shapes that connection and communication takes.

body:
In this way we come to feel at home in the world through our developing a deep sense of belonging to this Place and its People known as Kʼicheʼ Maya and the many Maya Amaqʼ that they name in their naming of the names of those who were there at the Dawn of their Sun. The One and Only Dawn experienced by all the Tribes-Amaqʼ who were their watching and waiting for the Sun, Moon, and Star at this Origin of the Kʼicheʼ Maya Sun.

These are the Original People of this Dawn that was experienced by all as their Dawn; People of Pueblos who came to live in this Sacred Landscape that comes to life through this Ancient Ancestral Account that awakens us to the wisdom that awaits us through walking this myth we come to live by in order to transcend the past in order to live empowered lives in this continuously transforming world. We are just about to enter this Sacred Landscape as reflected in the Imaginal Realm of this Mythic Masterpiece spoken of as the Ancient Word; Ancestral Account of Popol Wuj. The Dawn of the Kʼicheʼ Sun has risen and so the power and authority of Kʼicheʼ Maya Sovereignty and its Rule will now begin on the Mountain Top Citadel of Jaqawitz.

Jaqawitz There werenʼt many people in existence up there at the time; there were just a few of them living up on top of the mountain Jaqawitz. It was there where they met the Sun at Dawn. It was there atop Jaqawitz where they burnt their offerings. There on Jaqawitz the Sunrise shined bright for them at Dawn; there at Dawn the Sun rose upon Jaqawitz; Jaqawitz was the place of their Sun and its Dawn; and this is what made Jaqawitz their Dawning Place; their Dawning Place of their Sun. There in the East, there at the Coming Out Place of the Sun-chi Relebʼal Qʼij is where they walked away from when they walked away from the place of their origin there in Tolan Tzʼuy Wa. They were those who walked away from Tolan Tzuy-Wa to abandon it and that is how they came away from that place in the East known as the Relebʼal Qʼij.

That was their Mountain Place; that was their Place of the Plain; that was their Place of the Mountain-Place of the Plain: Juyubʼal, Taqʼajal, their Mountain; their Plain.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
Relebʼal Qʼij; there in the East at the Coming Out Place of the Sun was their Mountain Place; their Plain Place; Kijuyubʼal, Kitaqʼajal.

That was their Place of Origin; their Place of Sprouting Forth into the Sky- Earth known as their Mountain, their Plain: Juyubʼ, Taqʼaj. That is where they come from, those known as:

Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ, Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ, Majukʼutaj, Ikʼi Bʼalam

They grew there on the Mountain Top-Chuwi Juyubʼ; there up above on their Mountaintop is where they grew to become many, many people. Their fortified citadel-kitinamit-came forth there in that place on top of the Mountain- Chuwi Juyubʼ-where they built a palisade known as a kʼoxtun. That is where their Tinamit; Citadel was first made to be built up and brought forth; when their citadel-tinamit was built by a multiplying population of people; a growing population of people who lived there in a village-chinamit on top of the Mountain known as Chuwi Juyubʼ.

Tinamit is a walled enclosure while a Chinamit is a group of people or a village but the signification of these words seems to move about with changes of meaning depending on the way they are used and the context in which they are found.

A Tinamit can be used to talk about a Territory or a Realm or a Kingdom of a People when speaking of the Tinamit Kʼicheʼ one is speaking of the Kʼicheʼ Kingdom or the Realm of the Pueblo Kʼicheʼ.

Whereas chinamitl comes from the cane of maize or carrizo cane to signify a village that is enveloped by its milpa or chinamitl that is a cane enclosure or cane wall known as a chinampa a word derived from chinamitl. It is no small thing that mitl is an arrow used to defend the People of a Pueblo who are set upon from an attacking force from the outside. A chinamit also defines a group of people who make-up a village that lives within the fortification of a tinamit which is a fortified citadel that is defended with chimalli-shields-pokobʼ and mitl-arrows and tlacoltl-bow.

There upon Chuwi Juyubʼ is where they were when they appeared up above in the Sky overhead. It was there where they were at the time of their emergence; those that appeared were the Sun, Qʼij; the Moon, Ikʼ; and the Star, Chʼumil.

This was their place of emergence when they appeared there at Dawn; they appeared there when the Sun rose to light-up the Face of the Earth; when the light of the Sun lit-up and illuminate everything there was in existence beneath the Sky.

That is the place on the mountain top where their singing of their song began; Qamuku is the name of their song.

“¡Aqʼaroq! Ay de nosotros! We lost our way in Tulan, gone astray from one another we went our separate way in Tulan, in Tulan. It was there where we split- up, it was there we went our way, when we divided up and went astray from one another in Tulan, in Tulan.” “That was when we lost our way, when we lost our way in Tulan, in Tulan. It was there we left our Older Brothers abandoned when we left them there on their own in Tulan, in Tulan.” “It was there in Tulan, in Tulan where we left behind our Younger Brothers; when we left our Older Brothers; when we left them alone and moved on and moved; when we left our Young Brothers behind when we abandoned Tulan, when we left Tulan; we moved on; we moved on from Tulan, from Tulan.” “It was there we went wrong; we went wrong in Tulan, in Tulan! We went our own way when we moved on to leave our Older and Younger Brothers long gone, long gone; in Tulan, in Tulan.” “Where could it be that they watched and waited for the Dawn? Where were they when they saw the Dawn; where we they when they saw the emergence of the Sun; where were they when came the appearance of the Sun?” “Where could they have been at the Coming of the Dawn; when Dawn shone for all; when the Sun shone for all at Dawn; at Dawn; when the Sun came to shine upon us all; when the Sun shined upon us all; where were they at the Dawn; at the Dawn?”

“Where were they at the Coming of the Dawn, the Dawn; our Older Brothers, our Younger Brothers of Tulan, of Tulan?” sang the AjKʼixbʼ; sung the AjKʼajbʼ of the Yaqui Winaq when they sang that Sad Song; when they sang that Sad Song Qamuku; Qamuqu when they abandoned Tulan; Tulan; Tulan!

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
Qamuqu; Qamuku Qamuqu; Qamuku Qamuqu: Our Burial, Our Death and Burial, Qa-Our, Muquj-Burial to create a mourning song of departure, a sad weeping song of drinking; a sad song sung upon abandoning the place they once called home Our Drinking, Our Toasting: Qamuku. Qamuku: our vision, our sight, our seeing; Qamuku Our Sight that we lost when our eyes were veiled like mist on a mirror by Our Formers; Our Shapers who did not want us to see-muku as Kabʼawil can see close and far and through rock and trees and stones and mountains…Qamuku: what happen to our vision, we no longer can see our Older and Younger Brothers to known where they are and how they are! ¡Aqaroq! We never find out just exactly what Qamuqu means but it signifies many deep and important things when it comes to the Sowing and the Dawning because muqu is to sow seeds just as it is to bury the dead. And now that we have experienced the Dawning perhaps it is time to experience the Sowing; to bring forth the Sowing and Dawning.

Qamuqu is when the Maya milperos work their milpa after the last yearʼs harvest they must bury the dried-out rotten cane known as qʼumaraq aj. In this way last yearʼs leaf and canes are buried in long straight rows dried out, decimated, disintegrating rotten canes.

These canes are buried in long straight rows that that the workers of the milpa; Abʼixik who are very orderly working their milpa cover with earth to form and shape what look exactly alike long burial mounds about two varas wide and as long as the milpa which is traditionally a cuerda or kʼaʼm long. This long, relatively thin mound of buried cane is named just exactly what it looks like: Qamuqu, Our Burial.

body:
Once these long rows of buried cane are left to decompose for a month or more then the next yearʼs seed is sown in between the rows of ʼqamuquʼ so that the seed is sown down below in the trough formed and shaped between the rows of buried cane; rows of qamuqu where the moisture from the dew collects all night long. This is down in the trough or swale when and where the first rain falls to catch all the first downpours of Jun Raqan Jabʼ or One Footed Rain water that falls with the first rain fall. This is what qamuqu signifies when it comes to the milpa.

But sense Qamuqu is sung when thinking upon Tulan and how it all went wrong then perhaps it is a ʼdrinking songʼ meant to provoke tears of remembrance that bring on weeping and wailing of regret upon leaving oneʼs older and younger brothers behind in Tulan: Qamuquj as ʼourʼ drinking songs makes a great deal of sense since we have already been asked to drink to the telling of the names of the Fathers of Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

We must pause for a moment to attempt an understanding of what is going on here with this name Qamuqu that could mean many things but the text does not tell us assuming everyone will always know what it means to be singing our song Qamuku, or Qamuqu. There is the phrase used in this section when talking about who the ʼdeer skinsʼ must be protected because they are useful in hunting to deceive the prey that says: are e ri umuquwach; these are deceptive; these are for deception!

Qamuqu most likely signifies our being deceived at Tulan; Tolan; Tollan; Tullan but that doesnʼt mean this word doesnʼt mean all the other possible meaning because the ʼwordʼ itself is a form of ʼmetaphorʼ that shapes the idea of deception. And we are about to enter into a beguiling narrative of tricksterʼs deception. So allow the meaning to open up because they are meant to be multiple indeed! This maybe the most fascinating section of the Popol Wuj because the way that it is written is ʼcompletely otherʼ than anything else we have seen. No translation has clarified this and because of that we enter the rest of reading of the Popol Wuj confused as to ʼwho is whoʼ and why exactly they ʼdo what they doʼ so let us briefly bring forth what we know so you can move through your reading of Popol Wuj bolstered by our knowledge of language and custom that we know to be truer than true. This was written specifically for you and your deeper comprehension of this ancient ancestral song: Qamuqu or Qamuku. Qamuqu: Our Burial, Our Death and Burial, Qa-Our, Muquj-Burial to create a mourning song of departure, a sad weeping song of drinking song upon abandoning the place once called home Our Drinking, Our Toasting: Qamuku.

We never find out just exactly what Qamuqu means but it signifies many deep and important things when it comes to the Sowing and the Dawning because muqu is to sow seeds just as it is to bury the dead. And now that we have experienced the Dawning perhaps it is time to experience the Sowing; to bring forth the Sowing and Dawning. Sowing of the Kʼicheʼ Winaq, Kʼicheʼ Amaqʼ Chuwi Juyubʼ on the Mountain Top of Jaqawitz “Tojil was just the name of the Kabʼawil of the Yaki Winaq. Yolkwat Kitzalkwat is his name known as Heart of the Serpent Quetzalcoatl or in Maya Kʼicheʼ Ukʼuʼx Ulew Qʼuqʼumatz was the name of Yolkwat Kitzalkwat Quetzalcoatl back in Tulan.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
“It is just because the name of our deity Yolkwat Kitzalkwat is he who was our Kabʼawil when we split-up from one another back in Tulan; back there in Tzuy-Wa when we left our Kabʼawil behind in Tulan Tzuy-Wa. They left with us as one, we were all there together as one; just one and the same when we left with our brothers, when we left Tulan-Tzuy-Wa,” they said when they spoke with one another.

They remembered their Older Brothers; they remembered their Younger Brothers, the Yaki Winaq who watched the sunrise there in México, as it is called now. There was a few of those Méxica Yaki who stayed right there at the Coming Out Place of the Sun Relebʼal Qʼij.

Those who stayed there were the Tepew Oliman is their name. They are those known as the Sovereign Lords of Rubber Lands; they of the Noble Rule of the Lands of Rubber: Tepew Oliman.

This is the name of those of the rubber groves beside the water there on the Gulf Coast of Campeche; Gulf Coast of Tabasco as the Land of Rubber is known: Tepew Oliman.

“They became known as the Ones we Left Behind-Xeqakanaj kanoq,” they said, the First Four Fathers of the Kʼicheʼ known as AjKʼixb, AjKajbʼ. Great was the affliction that they suffered in their hearts; great was the suffering that afflicted their souls there upon the mountain of Jaqawitz.

They felt the same as those known as the Tamubʼ, Ilokabʼ. They were just there in the forest: kʼechelaj.

“Amaqʼ Tʼan, Amaqʼ Dan,” is the name of the Amaqʼ Tamubʼ; Pueblo Tamubʼ and it was their sacrificial priests, AjKʼixb, AjKajbʼ of the Tamubʼ who were there with their Kabʼawil who was also Tojil. There was just one name for the Kabʼawil of all three branches of the Kʼicheʼ Winaq, Kʼicheʼ People: Tojil.

body:
Tojil was the same name as the Kabʼawil of the Rabʼinalebʼ only these Rabʼinal People spoke of their Kabʼawil Tojil with a name that changed just a bit: Jun Toj, as it is said; the name of the deity of the Rabʼinalebʼ; the Kabʼawil of the Rabinal Winaq was Jun Toj; the day name Jun Toj, One Rain; One Storm; One Debt; One Sacrificial Debt. One drop of Blood; for one drop of water that is the sacrificial debt exchange between humanity and divinity Jun-Jun; One to One: Blood for Rain. And that is the reason they call him Jun Toj which is the name of Tojil among the Rabʼinalebʼ because their language known today as ʼAchiʼ was so very close to being the same as the other ʼKʼecheʼ language.

Maya Achi is the language known today as the spoken and written Kʼiche language of Rabinal. This language is were similar to the Kʼicheʼ of the Central Kʼiche but different enough to create a separate language that is known as Maya Achi of Rabinal where the Dance Drama of the Rabinal Achi continues to be danced out telling the story of Jun Toj similar to the way Dance Dramas were danced out long ago; similar to the long performance of this production of the Ancient Word; Ancestral Account of Popol Wuj.

But this is just what is said, because the Kʼicheʼ language that is spoken by the Rabʼinalebʼ is almost exactly the same as that which is spoken by the other Kʼicheʼ people.

Now what changes most is the speech spoken by the Qʼaqʼchekelebʼ or Kaqchikelebʼ and this is because of the difference in the name of the Kabʼawil when they left Tulan Tzuy-Wa.

Sotzʼi Ja Chimalkan is the name of their deity, because of this there is a difference in their ways of speech today. It is just because of the name of their deity that created the changes in the naming of their Pueblos; Chinamit known as the AjPop Sotzʼil, AjPop Xajil, as they are named, as they are known; the names of their Pueblos: AjSotzʼil, AjXajil; the People of the Bat; the People of the Dance. It is just their Kabʼawil that created the change in their speech, in their language. This happened when these people were given their Kabʼawil in Tulan.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
The language with which they spoke together changed the way the people, the Kaqchikel People, spoke with one another. It was their stone images of their Kabʼawil that caused the difference in speech, the speech of the stone images that the people were given; these were the stone images of the Kabʼawil that they carried away with them when they left Tulan in the dark of night amidst the darkness: Ta xpe Tulan chi qʼequmal.

But there was only One Sowing, One Dawning for all of the Pueblos. Xa kʼu Jun Xawax wi; Xa Jun Xsaqir wi ronojel Amaqʼ.

Yet each group that came away from Tulan came away with their Kabʼawil that spoke their own language; all of the Pueblos left with Kabʼawil that spoke their own form of speech. Now let us speak of the places where they stopped and stayed there on the mountain. In just one place were the four of them when they stopped to stay in a resting places on their way; their names were Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ, Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ, Majukʼutaj, Ikʼi Bʼalam; those were their names.

Their hearts wept for Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz who they left in the bromeliad; in the hanging moss in the great forest; in the deep canyon is where they left them;

their Kabʼawil were left hidden in their hideaways in the Hidden Canyon; Ewaxibʼal Siwan and the Great Mountain; Nimaʼ Kʼechelaj.

Origin of the veneration of Tojil This was when they went to perform sacrifice with their sacred fire where they gave sacrifice with burnt offerings. This was the origin of the veneration of Tojil; this was the beginning of their rituals of sacrifice when they came before the divine presence of Tojil, Awilix.

This was when they went to see them, to visit them in the forest, in the canyons; when they went to invoke them; to worship them; to give them thanks and gratitude; the show them praise and worship them there by prostrating themselves by bending down-low before them there in the forest at dawn.

It was just through their nawal presence that they spoke; that is to say through the Stone Images becoming ʼYoung Menʼ.

source: Popol Wuj: Complete Translation & Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (MARCH 24 2026 master PDF)
body:
The AjKʼixbʼ, AjKajbʼ took positions of reverence-wonowoj-kneeling down low ʼas ifʼ to demonstrate a traditional form of veneration through subjugation to oneʼs Divinity or oneʼs Kabʼawil. This was a traditional way of to show worship and veneration by kneeling down doubled-over there before their Kabʼawil; prostrating themselves before their Stone Images; Abʼajil as they were known. With their chin upon their knees- wonowoj to demonstrate the highest regard, deep respect for their Kabʼawil who they wished to show reverential adoration by worshipping them by providing them sweet, sweet smell offerings and to sustain them with burnt offering of sacrifice that were the sacrificial offerings they offered up in the round altars of sacrifice. These Stone Images-Abʼajil were there in the forest but now only their Nawal Spirit spoke to their AjKʼixbʼ, AjKʼajb who came before Tojil there in the Great Forest.

What the AjKʼixibʼ, AjKʼajibʼ brought with them to burn was no great gift; they just brought pine tree resin-qʼol and the blood of the Sun that bleeds as pine sap-xa rachaq noʼj from the wounding of Pine Trees. They brought these gifts along with Iyaʼ which is Pericón to burn before their Kabʼawil there where they made their Ceremonial Fire that was known as a Flower; Kotzʼij with the Power, Qʼaqʼal to change and transform both Sky and Earth.

The AjKʼixibʼ, AjKʼajibʼ burnt ʼjust pine resin, just pine sap; xa qʼol, xa rachaq noʼj along with pericón flowers-iyaʼ this is what they brought to the mountain to be burnt as sweet smelling, fragrant offerings of the Mountain-Plain; Juyubʼ-Taqʼaj; they brought them to be burnt there before Tojil their Kabʼawil. So now Tojil spoke through his Nawal to give the knowing that was the knowledge that he need to give the them his AjKʼixibʼ, AjKʼajibʼ
